prompt:
A job application has 6 steps. Step 2 asks for 'Current employer' and 'Job title.' Step 5, a 'Review your experience' summary, shows every field from step 2 except those two — leaving a blank 'Employer' text box for the applicant to fill in again from memory.

Is this a WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry problem?

options.text: No — a review screen is expected to ask for confirmation, not just display data
Yes — the values already exist in the flow's state and this screen doesn't reuse them
No, because it's only two fields out of many on the review screen
Only if the applicant actually gets the re-typed values wrong

hints: A 'review' screen is supposed to show what was entered, not silently drop two fields and ask for them again.
3.3.7 doesn't care how many other fields on the screen behaved correctly — a single field that forces re-entry without offering reuse is enough to fail it.
The criterion is about whether the mechanism to reuse exists at all, not about the eventual accuracy of what the user retypes.
explanation: Yes. A review screen exists specifically to display what's already been entered — one that silently omits two fields and re-asks for them, blank, breaks the entire pattern the rest of the screen sets up and forces the applicant to remember and retype values the system already has. The count of affected fields doesn't matter to the criterion; one is enough. This is also a case worth flagging as unusually confusing for the person filling it in, since a review screen implicitly promises 'here's what you told us,' and two blank required fields inside it read as a bug rather than a request.

prompt: A password-reset form asks the user to type their new password into two separate fields: 'New password' and 'Confirm new password.' A reviewer flags this as a 3.3.7 Redundant Entry violation. True or false?

config.statement: Asking for a password twice on a reset form is a genuine WCAG 3.3.7 violation.
config.rubric: A full answer names the specific exception 3.3.7 allows — re-entry that's essential — and explains why a password confirmation qualifies.

hints: 3.3.7 has a named exception for re-entry that's 'essential to the process.'
Think about what the second field is actually for — it isn't storing the same value twice for convenience, it's catching a typo the person can't otherwise see.
A masked password field hides what was typed, which is exactly why a second independent keystroke has a real purpose here that a name or address field doesn't.
explanation: False. WCAG 3.3.7 explicitly exempts re-entry where it's 'essential' — and a password confirmation field is the textbook case: the first field is masked, so the only way to catch a typo before submitting is an independent second entry, not a copy of the first. This is worth knowing precisely because it's the example someone will use to argue *against* a legitimate 3.3.7 finding elsewhere ('well, we ask for the address twice for the same reason') — the actual test is whether re-entry serves a purpose re-display can't, not whether re-entry happens at all.

prompt: A banking app's 2FA code field blocks paste and disables the `autocomplete` attribute, with a code comment reading 'security requirement, do not change — see ticket SEC-441.' Write the finding you'd actually log, given you don't have visibility into what SEC-441 says.
hints: You can log a real finding about user impact without knowing — or needing to know — the security team's exact reasoning.
Separate the observation (what happens to a keyboard/memory-limited user) from the recommendation (which should acknowledge you don't know if there's a deliberate trade-off here).
A good finding here asks a specific question rather than assuming the block is either purely accidental or fully justified.
explanation: A strong finding separates what you observed from what you're recommending, and is honest about the gap in your own information: *Users cannot paste or autofill the one-time code, forcing manual retyping of a 6-digit number read from a separate app, under this flow's 90-second countdown. This measurably increases both the time and error rate for anyone relying on working memory under load. A code comment references a security rationale (SEC-441) that isn't visible from the front end — recommend the security team confirm whether this is a deliberate, documented trade-off (in which case it should be named as one in the accessibility statement) or a default that was never revisited. If deliberate, request the ticket, since a legitimate reason and 'nobody thought about it' warrant different levels of urgency.* The point isn't to assume bad faith — some paste blocks really are chosen deliberately — it's to not quietly accept 'do not change' from a comment you can't verify, and to make the org either defend the trade-off or fix it.

prompt: Sort each of these into 'WCAG 3.2.1/3.2.2 violation' or 'real barrier, no clean 3.2 citation.'

items.text: A search filter checkbox that, the instant it's checked, opens a new browser tab with results and no warning
A cookie-consent banner sliding in from the bottom of the screen 3 seconds after page load, pushing all page content upward
A text field that, on receiving focus, immediately submits the surrounding form
A 'quantity' stepper on a product page whose plus/minus buttons visibly jump position when a promotional badge appears above them mid-interaction
Selecting a country from a dropdown that automatically navigates to that country's separate site with no confirmation

hints: 3.2.1/3.2.2 are about context changes: new window, navigation, submitting a form, moving focus somewhere unrequested — triggered by focus or input with no advance warning.
A banner that reflows the layout, without navigating anywhere or moving focus, sits outside the letter of these two criteria even when it's a genuine problem.
Ask specifically: did the *context* change (new page, new window, focus moved without being asked), or did the *layout* change while the context stayed the same?
explanation: The dividing line is exactly what changed: navigating to a new tab, submitting a form, or jumping to a different site are context changes triggered by focus or input, and WCAG requires the user be warned or in control of when that happens — that's 3.2.1/3.2.2 squarely. A banner sliding in or a button reflowing under it changes what's on screen without changing the context itself: no navigation, no submitted form, no focus jump. Both can genuinely disable someone — the reflow case can cause a real mis-click for someone with motor slowing or a tremor — but only the first category has a criterion written to catch it. The second belongs in a good audit as a named finding without a forced citation.

prompt: A design system audit finds the 'submit this form and stay on the page, showing a confirmation' pattern labelled three different ways across the product: 'Save changes,' 'Update,' 'Apply.' Put the fix steps in the order you'd actually do them.

items: Confirm all three buttons genuinely perform the identical function — same fields committed, same confirmation behaviour, nothing subtly different
Pick one label for the whole product, based on which reads clearest for the action (not which screen happens to have the most users)
Log it as one WCAG 3.2.4 finding covering all three instances, not three separate findings
Recommend updating the design system component itself, not each screen individually, so it can't drift apart again

hints: Before recommending a single label, verify the three buttons are actually the same function and not three different things that happen to look similar.
3.2.4 is about a single underlying pattern, so it's one finding with three locations, not three unrelated ones.
The most durable fix targets the shared component definition, not three separate screens that will just drift apart again next release.
explanation: Confirming true equivalence first matters because 3.2.4 only applies to components with the *same* functionality — if 'Apply' on the notifications screen actually does something subtly different (applies without navigating away, say), it isn't a consistency violation at all, it's a different action that happens to look similar, and mislabelling that as a 3.2.4 finding sends the fix in the wrong direction. Once equivalence is confirmed, the fix belongs at the component level: three screens hand-fixed today drift apart again the next time someone builds a fourth screen from a copy-pasted example instead of the shared component.

prompt: A signup form's email field has no visible label — just placeholder text reading 'you@example.com' inside the input. What's the most accurate description of the problem?

options.text: None — the placeholder makes the field's purpose obvious from the example format
The instruction (what to enter) disappears the moment the user types, and depending on markup it may not be reliably exposed to assistive tech as a label at all
The example email address itself might be someone's real address, which is a privacy issue
The placeholder text colour is definitely too light to pass contrast

hints: Ask what happens to this text the moment someone starts typing, and what a screen reader is guaranteed (or not guaranteed) to announce for a placeholder versus a real <label>.
'Obvious from context' is a sighted, first-glance judgement — it says nothing about what happens once text is entered or how a screen reader exposes it.
The two real problems are the same shape as the password example: disappears on input, and isn't a substitute for a proper <label> element.
explanation: Placeholder-only fields fail two ways at once, and it's worth being able to name both. First, the instruction vanishes on input — exactly the password-field mechanism from this lesson. Second, a placeholder is not the same thing as a `<label>` element: some screen reader and form-autofill combinations announce placeholder text as a hint, some don't announce it at all once the field has focus, and none of them treat it with the reliability of an associated `<label for="...">`. WCAG 3.3.2 wants a real, persistent instruction — which in practice means a visible `<label>`, with the placeholder left as an optional example layered on top, not a replacement for it.

prompt: A signup form shows password format requirements only inside the error message that appears after a failed submission attempt, never before. True or false: showing the requirement at all, even only after a failure, is sufficient to meet WCAG 3.3.2.

config.statement: Showing password requirements only after a failed submission satisfies WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that 3.3.2 requires instructions 'when content requires user input' — i.e. up front, not only as a consequence of getting it wrong.

hints: 3.3.2's wording is about instructions being provided when input is required — read that as a timing requirement, not just a presence requirement.
A requirement that only appears after failure has already cost the user one full wasted attempt by definition.
Technically 'present somewhere in the flow' and 'present when it's needed' are two different claims.
explanation: False. 3.3.2 requires instructions where content requires input — the natural reading is *before* or *during* entry, not exclusively as a punishment for getting it wrong the first time. A requirement that only surfaces after a failed submission has already guaranteed one wasted round trip: type, submit, get rejected, read the rule for the first time, retype while holding it in mind. That's a strictly worse experience than seeing the rule up front, and it's the specific pattern worth naming in a finding rather than settling for 'well, it's shown eventually.'

prompt: A 14-field registration form submits and shows a red banner at the top: 'Please correct the errors below.' No field is visibly marked, focus doesn't move, and there's no list of what's wrong. Write the finding.
hints: Name what's actually missing — not 'the error message is unhelpful' in general, but the specific pieces (location, focus, per-field marking) that are absent.
Cite both 3.3.1 (error identified) and 3.3.3 (suggestion, where a fix is knowable) if both genuinely apply here.
State what the user is left having to do themselves, since that's what makes the severity argument concrete.
explanation: A strong finding: *On submitting the registration form with invalid data, a banner reads 'Please correct the errors below' with no list of which fields are affected, no visual marking on the invalid fields themselves, and no focus movement — the user's viewport stays exactly where it was at the bottom of the page. They are left to manually re-scan all 14 fields to locate the problem before they can even begin fixing it. WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification (A): the item in error is not identified. WCAG 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (AA): no correction guidance is offered at all. Recommend: focus an error summary on submit, link each listed error to its field, and mark each invalid field with icon plus text, not colour alone.* The finding names the concrete missing pieces (location, focus, per-field marking) rather than a general complaint, which is what turns it into something a developer can implement without a follow-up conversation.

prompt: Match each field-clearing behaviour to whether it's a defensible security choice or a state-management defect.

pairs.left: Clearing a CVV field after a declined card payment
pairs.right: Defensible — sensitive value, shouldn't persist

pairs.left: Clearing a correctly-entered shipping address because the payment on the same page failed
pairs.right: Defect — unrelated field punished for a sibling's error

pairs.left: Clearing a security-question answer field after 3 failed attempts, to prevent guessing
pairs.right: Defensible — sensitive value, shouldn't persist

pairs.left: Resetting an entire multi-step wizard back to step 1 because step 4 had one validation error
pairs.right: Defect — unrelated field punished for a sibling's error

hints: Ask, for each: is there a genuine security or privacy reason not to retain this specific value, or is everything just being reset together because that was simpler to build?
Sensitive-value clearing is narrow and specific to that one field — it doesn't need to take unrelated fields down with it.
explanation: The pattern repeats: security-sensitive fields (payment codes, security-question answers under a guessing attack) have a real, narrow reason not to persist across a failure. Everything else that gets cleared alongside them — a shipping address, three prior steps of a wizard — has no such justification; it's collateral damage from resetting the whole form or flow as one unit rather than validating and clearing at the level of the individual field that actually failed.

prompt: A form's session times out after 20 minutes of inactivity, but at 18 minutes a dialog appears: 'Your session is about to expire. Stay logged in?' with a button to extend it. There's still no autosave — if the dialog is missed, all typed content is lost. Does this meet WCAG 2.2.1?

options.text: Yes — 2.2.1 only requires a warning and an extend option, both of which are present
No — 2.2.1 also requires autosave so nothing is ever lost
No — 18 minutes' warning isn't long enough

hints: Re-read exactly what 2.2.1 requires: warn, and let the user turn off/adjust/extend before expiry. Autosave is good practice but check whether it's actually inside the criterion's wording.
The criterion doesn't specify a minimum warning duration — it requires that a mechanism to extend exists before the limit is reached.
explanation: Yes, this meets 2.2.1 as written — a warning plus a working extend mechanism before the limit hits is exactly what the criterion asks for. It's worth being precise about this even though it feels incomplete: autosave is genuinely better practice and closes the remaining risk (someone stepping away from the screen entirely and missing the dialog), but it isn't what 2.2.1 requires, and a finding that claims otherwise stretches the citation past what it actually says. The honest version of this finding recommends autosave as a best-practice addition, cited separately from the (already-met) 2.2.1 compliance claim — conflating the two makes both claims weaker.

prompt: A product team says: 'We can't really design for cognitive accessibility the way we do for screen readers, because there's no testable WCAG success criterion for most of it — so it's not something we can put in a compliance report.' True or false: this is a fair reason not to include cognitive findings in an audit.

config.statement: The absence of a testable WCAG success criterion for most cognitive-accessibility guidance is a fair reason to leave those findings out of an audit report.
config.rubric: A full answer separates 'not independently testable against a numbered criterion' from 'not real or not worth reporting' — an audit can and should include evaluative findings without a citation.

hints: This lesson explicitly named the honest limit: some cognitive-accessibility guidance is advisory, not a Level A/AA criterion — but 'advisory' and 'not real' aren't the same claim.
Think back to the earlier finding in this module that had no clean 3.2 citation — was leaving it out of the audit the right call there?
What does a client actually need from an audit — a list of citations, or a list of things that will actually stop users completing tasks?
explanation: False. This lesson has already shown the pattern once, with layout shift and WCAG 3.2 — the absence of a numbered criterion doesn't mean the barrier isn't real or doesn't belong in the report, it means the finding gets written without a citation instead of with one. An audit whose only job is checking boxes against WCAG's numbered list will systematically under-report exactly the barriers this whole phase exists to cover — cognitive load, unclear content, sensory and energy cost. The honest version of a compliance report says plainly which findings are WCAG failures and which are evaluative, evidence-based findings outside WCAG's current scope — and includes both, because a user who can't complete the task doesn't experience the difference.

prompt: Sort each interface change into 'genuinely reduces cognitive load' or 'optimises a different metric and can increase it.'

categories: Optimises a different metric, can increase load

items.text: Splitting a dense settings page into labelled sections with clear headings
Removing a multi-step wizard's progress indicator because it 'adds visual noise'
items.category: Optimises a different metric, can increase load

items.text: Adding a persistent 'Save draft' that works at any point, not just at the end of a flow
Merging a 6-screen onboarding flow into 1 screen to cut the click count from 6 to 1
items.category: Optimises a different metric, can increase load

items.text: Replacing a wall of unlabelled checkboxes with grouped, named categories of 3-4 items each

hints: The genuine reductions all make it easier to know where you are, what's expected right now, and what's already safe — chunking, labelling, and protecting work in progress.
The false ones all trade a real cognitive cost for a metric that's easy to measure and put in a slide (click count, pixel density, visual noise) but doesn't track what actually taxes working memory.
explanation: The genuine reductions share a mechanism: they make it clearer what's expected right now, group related things into rememberable chunks, or remove a source of catastrophic loss someone would otherwise have to stay vigilant against. The false ones optimise something else entirely — fewer clicks, less visual noise, faster to build — and in doing so remove structure (chunking, a sense of place, orienting cues) that was actually doing cognitive work, even though it looked, at a glance, like simplification.

prompt: A tax-filing site's step 6 of 9 asks the user to 're-enter your National Insurance number to continue' — the same number entered on step 1, shown nowhere on screen. Which is the correct read?

options.text: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry violation — no re-entry mechanism is offered and this isn't security-essential in the way a password confirmation is
Not a violation — a National Insurance number is sensitive, so re-entry is justified like a CVV
Not testable without knowing whether browser autofill catches it

hints: Compare this to the CVV case from lesson 1 — what made CVV re-entry defensible was that storing it briefly was itself a security risk. Does that reasoning apply to a tax ID?
A National Insurance number is sensitive information, but sensitivity alone doesn't create the same 'shouldn't be retained even briefly in this session' justification a payment code has.
explanation: This is a 3.3.7 violation. Sensitivity isn't the same test as the CVV exception — a CVV shouldn't be retained even momentarily because storing payment codes is itself a security anti-pattern regardless of re-entry; a National Insurance number, already validated and safely held in the session's own state for the other 8 steps of this exact flow, has no equivalent reason to force a blind retype three steps later. This is the trap version of the CVV lesson: 'it's sensitive' sounds like it should excuse re-entry, but the actual test is whether persisting it *within this session, this flow* creates a risk — not whether the data is generally sensitive.

prompt: A mobile app's 'Add payment method' sheet grows taller as validation messages appear beneath each field, pushing the 'Confirm' button further down the screen — but this only happens after the user taps Confirm once, not while they're still typing. True or false: this avoids the layout-shift problem from this module.

config.statement: Because the layout only shifts after a tap, not during typing, this avoids the layout-shift barrier discussed in this module.
config.rubric: A full answer notes the shift still displaces a target (Confirm) right as the user is likely to tap it again, regardless of whether it happened during typing or after a first tap.

hints: The barrier isn't specifically about typing — it's about a control moving right as someone is about to interact with it again.
After a failed first tap, where is the user's attention and, often, their finger or pointer? Right where Confirm used to be.
explanation: False. The mechanism is the same regardless of what triggered it: Confirm moves right as the user, having just tapped it once and likely about to tap it again after noticing an error, is aiming for where it was. Timing the shift to 'after a tap' instead of 'during typing' doesn't remove the barrier — it just changes which moment it hits. The actual fix from this module still applies: reserve space for validation messages so the layout doesn't reflow underneath a control someone is about to use again.

prompt: Match each real product pattern to the WCAG criterion (or 'no clean citation') it belongs under.

pairs.left: A dropdown auto-submits and navigates the moment a new option is selected, with no warning
pairs.right: 3.2.2 On Input

pairs.left: The same 'delete' action is an icon-only trash can on one screen and a text button labelled 'Remove' on another
pairs.right: 3.2.4 Consistent Identification

pairs.left: A promotional badge appears above a product's 'Add to cart' button mid-scroll, shifting it down as the user reaches for it
pairs.right: No clean citation

pairs.left: A billing address field is left blank with no option to copy the shipping address entered two screens earlier
pairs.right: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry

hints: Auto-submit-and-navigate on a mere selection is squarely a context-change criterion.
A layout shift with no navigation and no focus change is the same 'real barrier, no clean citation' pattern from earlier in this module.
explanation: The dropdown case is a direct 3.2.2 violation — selecting an option is 'input,' and navigating away from it with no warning is exactly the context change the criterion exists to prevent. The icon-vs-text delete action is 3.2.4: same function, inconsistent identification. The billing-address case is the textbook 3.3.7 pattern from lesson 1. The scrolling badge case has no criterion written for it — it's a layout shift, not a context change — and belongs in a report as a named finding without a forced citation, the way this module has modelled twice already.

prompt: A form clears entirely and shows a generic 'Something went wrong' message with no field marking after a submission error. Put the redesign steps in a sensible priority order — most important fix first.

items: Stop clearing valid field values on any single field's error
Move focus to a specific error summary naming what's wrong
Mark each invalid field individually, with icon and text, not colour alone
Add a persistent (not placeholder-only) instruction for any field with a format requirement

hints: Losing all typed data is the most costly single failure in the list — fixing it first prevents the worst outcome even before the rest is addressed.
Once data isn't being destroyed, the next priority is making the actual errors findable, then identifiable per field, then preventable in the first place.
explanation: There's no single 'correct' priority order in the abstract, but data loss is the most expensive failure by cost-to-the-user, which is why it leads: someone who loses all 12 fields' worth of typing is worse off than someone who has to locate one clearly-marked error. Once nothing is being destroyed, findability (focus + summary) and identifiability (per-field marking) come next because they determine how much extra work fixing the error costs. Preventing the error in the first place (persistent instructions) is valuable but addresses a smaller share of the pain once the other three are fixed.

prompt: A government portal's session times out after 10 minutes, with a warning dialog appearing at 8 minutes offering to extend. There's no autosave. A user steps away for a phone call at minute 7, misses the dialog entirely, and returns at minute 12 to a logged-out screen with all typed content gone. Does this scenario reveal a WCAG 2.2.1 violation?

options.text: Yes — losing all the typed content is itself the violation
No — 2.2.1's specific requirements (warn, allow extend) were met; the remaining risk is a best-practice gap (autosave), not a citable failure
Yes, because 8 minutes isn't enough warning for a real interruption like a phone call

hints: This is the same distinction from lesson 4 — re-read what 2.2.1 actually requires versus what would additionally help.
A criterion can be technically met and a real, painful failure can still happen — those aren't contradictory statements.
explanation: No 2.2.1 violation — the warning and extend mechanism existed and worked as designed; the user missing it during an unrelated interruption doesn't retroactively fail a criterion that was correctly implemented. This is a genuinely uncomfortable but important distinction to hold: the interface did everything 2.2.1 requires, and someone still lost real work, because 2.2.1 doesn't require autosave and autosave is the only thing that would have protected this specific user. The right recommendation names autosave as a best-practice addition on top of already-compliant behaviour, not as a fix for a citation that doesn't actually apply.

prompt: Sort each dashboard change into 'reduces cognitive load' or 'optimises a different metric.'

items.text: Grouping 20 settings into 4 clearly labelled sections of about 5 each
Collapsing 4 settings sections into one flat list 'to reduce the number of taps to expand a section'
Adding a visible 'last saved 2 minutes ago' indicator to a long-form editor
Removing confirmation dialogs entirely so every change saves instantly, with no way to review before it commits

hints: Chunking into labelled groups and giving visible reassurance that work is safe both directly reduce what has to be tracked or worried about.
Flattening a list to save taps, or removing a review step to save time, both optimise speed/efficiency at the cost of something that was actually protecting the user's mental state or their work.
explanation: The genuine reductions make state visible and structure legible — grouped settings are easier to scan and remember than one long flat list, and a save-status indicator removes the low-grade anxiety of not knowing whether work is protected. The other two chase efficiency metrics (fewer taps, faster saves) at a real cost: a flattened list removes the chunking that made 20 items navigable, and removing confirmation removes the one moment someone could catch a mistake before it becomes permanent.

prompt: A hotel booking site's date picker recalculates and re-renders the entire calendar grid (shifting every date's on-screen position) every time the user hovers over a date, to show a live price preview. Write the finding.
hints: Think about who this actually stops, and what it costs them specifically — not just 'this is annoying.'
Consider whether there's a clean WCAG citation here or whether, like earlier in this module, this belongs as a named finding without one.
explanation: A strong finding: *Hovering over any date in the calendar triggers a full re-render that shifts every date cell's position (to accommodate a live price tooltip), meaning the date the user is currently moving toward can move out from under the pointer before the click lands — most likely to cause a mis-click for anyone with motor slowing, tremor, or who is deliberately moving carefully to conserve effort. This isn't a WCAG 3.2 context-change failure (no navigation or focus change occurs) and has no clean citation, but it directly costs task completion for a real group of users. Recommend: keep the calendar grid's layout fixed regardless of hover state, showing the price preview in a separate, fixed-position area instead of one that displaces the grid itself.* This mirrors the layout-shift pattern from lesson 2 in a genuinely different surface — the point of naming it without forcing a citation is that the finding's usefulness doesn't depend on which WCAG number it's filed under.

prompt: A password-reset flow shows the format requirement as static, always-visible text below the field (not a placeholder), and also repeats it inside the error message if validation fails. True or false: repeating the requirement in the error message, on top of the always-visible text, is redundant and should be removed.

config.statement: Repeating the password requirement inside the error message, when it's already always visible below the field, is redundant and should be cut.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes this from placeholder-based redundancy — this is genuine reinforcement at the moment of failure, not the only copy of the information, and isn't the timing problem this module identified.

hints: This is a different situation from the placeholder case — ask whether the requirement is genuinely disappearing anywhere, or whether it's simply stated twice.
Reinforcing a requirement exactly at the moment someone needs to act on it (right after a failed attempt) is a different thing from the requirement only existing at that moment.
explanation: False. This isn't the placeholder problem — the requirement is always visible regardless of what triggers the error message, so nothing is disappearing at the point of need. Repeating it inside the error message reinforces it at exactly the moment it's most relevant (right after getting it wrong), which is reasonable redundancy, not a redundant-entry-style tax on the user. The distinction worth holding onto: this module's actual target is instructions that are missing or vanish when needed, not every instance of the same text appearing twice.

prompt: A prescription label's original text reads: 'Take one tablet by mouth twice daily with food; do not discontinue without consulting your physician.' A rewrite reads: 'Take it however feels right for you.' Is the rewrite better plain language?

options.text: Yes — it's much shorter and easier to read
No — it deletes the actual dosage, timing and the warning against stopping suddenly, none of which are safe to omit
Yes, because medical instructions are always too complex to simplify
It depends only on the reading level score each version gets

hints: Compare what information exists in each version, not just how each one reads.
A dosage instruction that's missing the dose, the timing, and a real safety warning isn't simpler — it's a different, more dangerous document.
Plain language keeps necessary information and changes how it's said, not whether it's said at all.
explanation: The rewrite is not better plain language — it's a different, unsafe document. It deletes the dose ('one tablet'), the frequency ('twice daily'), the food requirement, and a genuine safety warning against stopping suddenly, none of which are optional information on a prescription label. Genuine plain language for this label would keep every one of those facts and restate them more simply: 'Take 1 tablet twice a day, with food. Don't stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.' That version is both shorter than the original and still contains everything the original did — which is the actual test, not length alone.

prompt: WCAG 3.1.5 Reading Level is an AAA success criterion that almost no organisation formally commits to meeting. True or false: this means plain-language failures don't belong in a real accessibility audit.

config.statement: Because 3.1.5 is AAA and rarely a formal target, plain-language problems don't belong in an accessibility audit.
config.rubric: A full answer separates 'not a mandatory numbered target' from 'not real or not worth reporting' — an audit can include evaluative plain-language findings without a mandatory citation, the same honest pattern used for cognitive-load findings without a clean WCAG number.

hints: This is the same honest-limits pattern from the previous module's cognitive-load lesson — an AAA or uncited finding isn't the same as a non-finding.
Think about what a client needs from an audit: a list of citations, or a list of things that actually stop people completing the task.
explanation: False. 3.1.5 being AAA affects whether it's a mandatory conformance target, not whether the underlying barrier is real. A denial letter nobody can parse still stops someone acting on it whether or not 3.1.5 is the organisation's formal target — the honest version of an audit reports plain-language findings as evaluative, clearly distinguished from mandatory A/AA failures, rather than omitting them because the citation is AAA or uncertain. This is the same principle the cognitive-accessibility module already established for layout shift and brain fog.

prompt: Rewrite this sentence, keeping every piece of information it contains: 'In the event of a Qualifying Life Event, Enrollees must submit documentation substantiating eligibility within thirty (30) calendar days of the Event Date, absent which coverage modifications shall not be effected retroactively.'
hints: Find the buried verb first — what is the sentence actually asking someone to do?
Split the trigger, the requirement, the deadline and the consequence into separate sentences.
Keep all four pieces of information: what counts as the trigger, what to submit, the 30-day deadline, and what happens if you miss it.
explanation: A strong rewrite: *If your life situation changes in a way that qualifies you for a coverage update (for example, marriage, a new child, or losing other coverage), tell us within 30 days and send proof (like a marriage certificate or birth certificate). If you wait longer than 30 days, we can't backdate the change to when the event actually happened.* This keeps all four original pieces of information — the trigger, the requirement, the deadline, the consequence — and states each one in its own sentence with a plain, active verb. The length isn't dramatically shorter; the point isn't brevity, it's that each sentence now carries exactly one idea instead of stacking four inside one nominalised, passive clause.

prompt: Sort each link's text into 'purpose determinable from link text alone (2.4.9)' or 'purpose only determinable from surrounding context (2.4.4 at best).'

categories: Purpose determinable from link text alone
Purpose only determinable from surrounding context

items.text: 'Download the March 2024 pricing PDF (1.2MB)'
items.category: Purpose determinable from link text alone

items.text: 'Learn more' at the end of a product description paragraph
items.category: Purpose only determinable from surrounding context

items.text: 'View your March invoice'
items.category: Purpose determinable from link text alone

items.text: 'Here' inside the sentence 'For our refund policy, click here'
items.category: Purpose only determinable from surrounding context

items.text: 'Compare the Standard and Premium plans'
items.category: Purpose determinable from link text alone

hints: Read each link text completely on its own, with no surrounding sentence — does it say where it goes or what it does?
'Here' and 'Learn more' are the two most common context-dependent link texts in real products, worth spotting immediately.
explanation: Links that name their destination or action inside the link text itself — 'Download the March 2024 pricing PDF,' 'View your March invoice,' 'Compare the Standard and Premium plans' — pass 2.4.9 and survive being pulled into a link list with no context. 'Learn more' and 'here' both depend entirely on the sentence around them to mean anything, and both are the two most frequently repeated context-dependent link texts across real products, which is exactly what makes a page with several of either one fail so badly in link-list navigation specifically.

prompt: A settings page has three 'Delete' buttons in a row — one each for 'Delete photo,' 'Delete account,' and 'Delete payment method' — all with the same visible text 'Delete' and no distinguishing markup. What's the most accurate fix?

options.text: Change the visible text on each button so a sighted user reads three different words
Give each button a distinct accessible name (visually-hidden text or aria-label naming what it deletes) while keeping the same short visible label for sighted users
Nothing needs to change — three 'Delete' buttons on the same page is fine as long as they're visually separated
Remove two of the three buttons to avoid duplication

hints: The visible text doesn't need to change for sighted users — sighted users have visual context (headings, layout) telling them apart already.
The fix is adding disambiguating context to the accessible name specifically, not rewriting what's visually on the page.
explanation: The right fix adds a distinct accessible name to each button — visually-hidden text like 'Delete photo' or an equivalent aria-label — while the visible text stays exactly 'Delete' for every sighted user, who already has layout and headings to tell the buttons apart. Rewriting the visible text unnecessarily changes a UI that works fine visually; removing buttons deletes real functionality. The actual gap is specifically in what a screen reader announces when a button is pulled out of its visual layout, and the fix targets that gap precisely.

prompt: A signup form rejects an email address with the message 'Invalid email' — correctly placed beneath the field, with focus correctly moved there. What's still missing?

options.text: Nothing — correct placement and focus movement satisfy the whole requirement
A specific statement of what's wrong with the entered value and what format is expected — 'Invalid email' identifies that an error exists without suggesting any fix
A louder color for the error text
An audio alert alongside the visual message

hints: This is the same distinction from the lesson's opening: placement (3.3.1-adjacent) and content (3.3.3) are separate obligations.
Ask what a reader can actually do differently after reading 'Invalid email' — the answer is nothing, because no rule is stated.
explanation: 'Invalid email' is correctly placed and correctly focused, and still fails to suggest any fix — the reader has no way to know whether the problem is a missing @ symbol, an unsupported domain, extra spaces, or something else entirely. A message like 'Enter your email in the format name@example.com — we couldn't find the @ symbol in what you typed' does what 3.3.3 actually asks: it names the specific expected format and the specific thing that was missing, giving the reader something to act on immediately rather than a guess-and-resubmit loop.

prompt: A form field rejects input with the message 'This field is required.' The field is actually a date-of-birth field, and the real reason for rejection is that the entered date is in the future, not that it was left blank. Write the finding and the correct rewrite.
hints: Notice that the message describes the wrong failure entirely — that's a more serious problem than a vague message.
The finding should name both that the message is generic and that it's factually incorrect for this specific case.
The rewrite should state the actual rule (a date of birth can't be in the future) and, ideally, echo back what was actually entered.
explanation: A strong finding: *The date-of-birth field shows 'This field is required' when a value is present but invalid (a future date) — the message describes a different failure (blank field) than the one that actually occurred, which is worse than a vague message because it actively points the user at the wrong problem to fix. This 3.3.3 failure isn't just about missing detail, it's about incorrect detail.* The rewrite: *'Your date of birth can't be in the future — you entered [date]. Please check the year.'* This names the actual rule that failed, references what was actually typed, and gives a concrete next step, rather than reusing a generic 'required field' message that happens to be technically false for this specific error.

prompt: A login form's error message says 'Incorrect email or password' rather than specifying which of the two was wrong. True or false: this is a content-quality defect that should be rewritten to name the specific field that failed.

config.statement: A login error that doesn't say whether the email or the password was wrong is a defect that should be fixed by naming the specific field.
config.rubric: A full answer names the account-enumeration security reason this vagueness is often deliberate, and treats it as a named trade-off rather than an automatic defect — the same pattern as the paste-blocking caveat from the previous module.

hints: This is a different case from the password-format example earlier in the lesson — ask whether specificity here could reveal something it shouldn't.
Think about what an attacker could learn from a message that specifically said 'that email doesn't have an account' versus 'that password is wrong for this account.'
explanation: False, without more information — and that qualifier is the actual point. Deliberately vague login errors are a common, legitimate security decision: specifying which field failed lets an attacker enumerate which email addresses have real accounts, one guess at a time. This is a genuine trade-off between usability and a real security property, not automatically a content defect, and it should be logged as a named trade-off — the same way the previous module's paste-blocking caveat was — rather than rewritten on sight or dismissed as an oversight without checking whether it's deliberate.

prompt: A rewritten health-result page scores several grade levels lower on an automated readability tool than the original. Does that score alone confirm the page is now genuinely clear to a first-time patient?

options.text: Yes — a lower readability score is definitive proof of genuine clarity
No — the score measures sentence length and syllable count only, and can't detect short jargon words or content that was deleted rather than clarified
No, because readability scores only apply to legal documents, not health content

hints: Think about what a readability formula actually counts — words, syllables, sentence length — versus what it has no way to measure.
A word like 'PCP' or 'afib' scores as easy by syllable count while being genuine jargon to a first-time reader.
explanation: A lower score is a useful, necessary signal, not sufficient proof of genuine clarity. Readability formulas count syllables and sentence length; they have no way to detect a short jargon word like 'PCP' or 'afib' scoring as 'easy,' and no way to tell whether the improved score came from genuinely clarifying the content or from quietly deleting the harder parts of it. A real clarity check needs both the score and a check for undefined jargon and deleted meaning — the score alone answers a narrower question than it looks like it does.

prompt: Match each method to what it actually reveals about a piece of copy.

pairs.left: An automated readability score
pairs.right: Sentence length and syllable count — not jargon or deleted meaning

pairs.left: Testing copy with someone outside the writing team's domain
pairs.right: Whether a genuine outsider can actually follow it, including jargon insiders no longer notice

pairs.left: Tracking 'what does this mean' support tickets over time
pairs.right: A real, ongoing signal of exactly which terms the actual audience is getting stuck on

pairs.left: A colleague from an adjacent team reviewing the copy
pairs.right: A check that's still likely to miss jargon shared across both teams' domains

hints: Only one of these methods draws its signal directly from the real, external audience rather than from inside the organisation.
An adjacent-team reviewer is closer to a real outsider than the original author, but not the same thing as one.
explanation: The readability score measures a narrow, mechanical property of the text itself. A genuine outside tester and real support-ticket data both draw their signal from people who aren't fluent in the organisation's internal vocabulary, which is exactly the blind spot that produces jargon nobody inside the team can see. An adjacent-team colleague is a real improvement over no outside review at all, but still shares enough context with the writer's world to miss the same jargon a true outsider would catch immediately.

prompt: An infographic-style image shows a bar chart with exact percentage values that appear nowhere else on the page. The developer writes alt="Chart showing survey results." Is this sufficient?

options.text: Yes — the alt text correctly identifies that a chart is present
No — this is a complex image, and identifying that a chart exists isn't the same as providing the actual data it contains; the real numbers need to exist as text somewhere on the page
Yes, as long as the chart has good color contrast

hints: Ask what a screen reader user learns from this alt text versus what a sighted user learns from looking at the chart directly.
'A chart exists' and 'here is what the chart says' are two different pieces of information — this alt text only provides the first.
explanation: This is insufficient. A complex image — a chart, graph or diagram carrying real data — needs its actual content provided as an accessible equivalent, not just a label confirming a chart is present. 'Chart showing survey results' tells a screen reader user that data exists and gives them none of it, while a sighted user reads the real percentages directly off the image. The fix is publishing the underlying values as real text or an HTML table near the image, with the alt text (or a caption) pointing to it, not attempting to cram every number into the alt attribute itself.

prompt: A team decides that, to be safe, every image on their site — including purely decorative background textures — should get a full, detailed alt text description rather than an empty alt. True or false: this is the safer, more accessible choice.

config.statement: Giving every image, including purely decorative ones, a full detailed alt description is the safer and more accessible default.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that a decorative image should get alt="" (empty, not missing) so it's skipped entirely, and that describing it in detail adds real listening-time cost for zero information.

hints: 'Safe' isn't the same as 'more detail is always better' — think about the actual cost of a screen reader announcing a long description for something with no content value.
An empty alt (alt="") is a deliberate, correct choice for decorative images — it isn't the same thing as leaving the alt attribute out entirely.
explanation: False. Describing a purely decorative image in detail costs a screen reader user real listening time for information that contributes nothing to the page — the same over-description problem this lesson names directly. The correct, deliberate choice for a genuinely decorative image is an empty alt (alt=""), which tells assistive technology to skip the image entirely rather than announce it at all. This is different from omitting the alt attribute altogether, which can cause some screen readers to announce the image's filename instead — empty alt is a real, specific decision, not an absence of one.

prompt: A gym membership cancellation flow's final confirmation reads: 'Your termination request has been processed and will be effectuated at the conclusion of the current billing cycle.' Which rewrite is genuine plain language rather than oversimplification?

options.text: 'Done!'
'Your membership will end on [date] — the last day of your current billing period. You won't be charged again after that.'
'We've processed your request.'

hints: The original states two things: that the cancellation is confirmed, and exactly when it takes effect.
A genuine rewrite keeps both facts in plain words — a real date, and a real statement about future billing.
explanation: The correct rewrite keeps both pieces of real information the dense original contains — that the request is confirmed, and specifically when it takes effect — stated in plain, concrete words with an actual date rather than a vague reference to 'the current billing cycle.' 'Done!' and 'We've processed your request' are both shorter, and both delete the one fact ('when does this actually end, and will I be charged again') the reader most needs from a cancellation confirmation.

prompt: Sort each link/button label into 'purpose clear from its own text' or 'purpose depends on surrounding context.'

categories: Purpose clear from its own text

items.text: 'Add Sarah Chen to your team'
items.category: Purpose clear from its own text

items.text: 'More'
'Export this report as CSV'
items.category: Purpose clear from its own text

items.text: 'Go'
'Renew your Premium subscription'
items.category: Purpose clear from its own text

hints: Read each label as if it were the only text on the page — does it say what will happen?
'More' and 'Go' are both classic context-dependent labels that fail identically in a button or link list.
explanation: Labels that name the specific object and action inside the text itself — who's being added, what format is being exported, which subscription is renewing — survive being read completely out of context. 'More' and 'Go' carry no information about what they do on their own; both depend entirely on nearby text or layout that a link/button list navigation strips away.

prompt: A file-upload field rejects a file with the message 'Upload failed.' Write the finding and a corrected message, assuming the actual cause (visible in dev tools but not to the user) is that the file exceeded a 5MB size limit.
hints: The gap here isn't placement — it's that the message gives zero information about which of many possible upload failures actually happened.
A specific rewrite states the actual limit and, ideally, the size of the file that was rejected.
explanation: A strong finding: *'Upload failed' is shown for every possible upload failure — wrong file type, size limit, network error — with no way for the user to tell which one occurred or what to do differently. This satisfies 3.3.1 only in the loosest sense (something is identified) and fails 3.3.3 completely, since no fix is suggested.* Rewrite: *'This file is too large. The limit is 5MB — your file is 8.2MB. Try compressing it or choosing a smaller file.'* This names the actual constraint, states the specific numbers involved, and gives a concrete next action, instead of leaving the user to guess between several unrelated possible causes.

prompt: A support article uses the term 'two-factor authentication' throughout, fully spelled out and never abbreviated to '2FA,' aimed at a general consumer audience who may never have set it up before. True or false: this term itself, even spelled out, still needs a plain-language definition the first time it's used.

config.statement: Spelling out 'two-factor authentication' in full is sufficient on its own — no additional plain-language definition is needed.
config.rubric: A full answer notes that spelling out a term isn't the same as defining it — someone unfamiliar with the concept doesn't automatically understand it just because it isn't abbreviated.

hints: Spelling out a term avoids one problem (an opaque abbreviation) without solving a different one (the reader still might not know what the concept means).
Think about the earlier lesson's test: would the actual audience already know this, regardless of whether it's abbreviated.
explanation: False. Writing 'two-factor authentication' in full instead of '2FA' avoids the abbreviation problem, but doesn't automatically explain the concept — someone who has never set it up may not know what it means even spelled out completely. A brief definition on first use ('two-factor authentication, or 2FA — a second check, like a code sent to your phone, in addition to your password') does what spelling it out alone can't: it explains the concept itself, not just avoids shortening its name.

prompt: A weather alert icon (a triangle with an exclamation mark) sits next to the text 'Severe weather warning in effect for your area' and is also itself a link to the full alert details. What should its alt text be?

options.text: alt="Warning triangle icon" — describing the icon's shape
alt="" (empty) — since the adjacent text already says the same thing, and the icon plus text together form one link to the full alert
A full paragraph describing the icon's color and design

hints: This icon is functioning as part of a link whose text already states the same information the icon represents.
When an icon sits beside text that already conveys the same meaning, and both are part of one control, the icon itself typically needs no separate alt text at all.
explanation: Because the icon sits inside a link alongside text that already states the warning ('Severe weather warning in effect for your area'), giving the icon its own alt text would just repeat the same information a second time in the same control's accessible name. Empty alt (alt="") is correct here — the link's accessible name is carried entirely by the adjacent text, and the icon is functioning as a decorative visual reinforcement of information already stated in words. Describing the icon's shape or color would add nothing a screen reader user needs and would repeat the warning redundantly within one link's name.

prompt: Put these steps in order for rewriting a piece of interface copy that's both jargon-heavy and structurally dense.

items: Find the buried verb and state the actual action plainly
Split any sentence carrying more than one rule into separate sentences
Define any genuinely necessary technical term once, in plain words, rather than deleting it
Check the rewrite against the original for anything accidentally deleted, not just shortened

hints: Structural fixes (finding the verb, splitting sentences) come before vocabulary fixes, because a badly structured sentence is often the reason the jargon feels even denser than it is.
The final check is what catches an oversimplified rewrite before it ships — always compare back against the original.
explanation: Structural work comes first because a nominalised verb and a stacked multi-rule sentence make everything inside them harder to follow, jargon included — untangling structure often makes the actual vocabulary problem easier to see and smaller than it first appeared. Necessary jargon then gets a definition, not a deletion. The final comparison against the original is what catches the specific failure mode this whole module keeps returning to: a rewrite that looks cleaner because something real was quietly removed.

prompt: A checkout page shows a coupon-code field. Entering an expired code produces the message 'Code error.' Write the finding and a corrected message.
hints: 'Code error' could mean the code is expired, misspelled, already used, or not valid for this cart — name the actual cause if it's determinable.
The rewrite should state the specific reason and a specific next step, not just repeat that something went wrong.
explanation: A strong finding: *'Code error' covers at least four different real causes — expired, misspelled, already redeemed, or not valid for the current cart contents — and gives the user no way to tell which applies, or what to try next. This fails 3.3.3 even though something is technically displayed near the field.* Rewrite, assuming the system knows the code expired: *'This code expired on [date]. Check your email for a current offer, or continue without a code.'* Naming the specific reason (expired, with the actual date) and a specific next step turns a dead end into something the shopper can actually act on immediately.

prompt: A hospital's post-surgery discharge instructions score at a university reading level on an automated tool but use only short, common words throughout ('Take your medicine. Rest. Call us if you have pain.'). True or false: a low readability score alone is proof the discharge instructions are missing necessary detail, not proof they're genuinely clear.

config.statement: Short sentences and common words alone guarantee that discharge instructions are genuinely clear and complete.
config.rubric: A full answer notes that short, simple sentences can still omit necessary specific detail (which medicine, how much, what pain level warrants a call) — brevity and completeness are different properties, mirroring the module's core distinction in the opposite direction from usual.

hints: This flips the module's usual direction — instead of dense text hiding meaning, ask whether short text might be hiding it by omission.
'Take your medicine' and 'call us if you have pain' are both too vague to act on safely, regardless of how simple the words are.
explanation: False. Short sentences and common words are necessary for plain language, not sufficient for it — 'Take your medicine' doesn't say which medicine, how much, or when; 'call us if you have pain' doesn't say what level of pain warrants a call versus normal post-surgery discomfort. A discharge instruction this vague can score easily on any readability tool while still failing the patient by omitting exactly the specific detail a plain-language rewrite is supposed to preserve. The fix keeps the short sentences and adds the missing specifics: 'Take 1 ibuprofen (200mg) every 6 hours if needed. Call us if your pain gets worse instead of better, or if you have a fever over 38°C.'

prompt: A recipe app's ingredient list has each item slide in with a bounce effect as the user scrolls down the page, purely for visual style. Under WCAG 2.3.3, what does this interface need?

options.text: Nothing — bounce effects are too minor to matter
A way to disable the scroll-triggered bounce animation, since it's interaction-triggered and has no function beyond visual style
The animation needs to be removed for every user, not made optional
A warning before the page loads that it contains animation

hints: Ask whether removing the bounce effect would change what the ingredient list communicates or does — it wouldn't.
The fix for non-essential interaction-triggered motion is making it disable-able, not removing it for every user.
explanation: This bounce-in effect is interaction-triggered (scrolling) and purely decorative — removing it changes nothing about the ingredient list's information or function. WCAG 2.3.3 requires a way to disable this kind of motion, not its outright removal for everyone, which would take away a stylistic choice most users have no problem with. The fix is typically respecting a prefers-reduced-motion preference, scoped correctly so it only removes decorative motion like this and not any essential feedback elsewhere on the page.

prompt: A team implements reduced-motion support by identifying every purely decorative animation individually and disabling only those under prefers-reduced-motion, leaving a small pulsing dot loading indicator untouched. True or false: this is a better implementation than a universal `* { animation: none }` rule.

config.statement: Scoping prefers-reduced-motion to decorative animation specifically, while preserving a small, functional loading indicator, is a better implementation than disabling all animation universally.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that a universal rule removes essential feedback (like loading state) along with decoration, and that a scoped rule keeps the essential information intact while still removing what could trigger symptoms.

hints: Think about what a user who enabled reduced motion still needs to know — is 'nothing is currently loading' the same information as 'this page is frozen'?
The goal is removing motion that could trigger symptoms, not removing every visual signal on the page.
explanation: True. A scoped implementation keeps essential motion — like a small, low-amplitude loading indicator — functioning, so a user with reduced motion enabled still knows whether the page is working or stuck, while removing decorative motion that serves no functional purpose. A universal `animation: none` rule treats both as equally disposable, which silently removes real information (loading state) exactly when the user most needs it, on top of achieving the intended goal for the decorative motion.

prompt: A stock-ticker banner scrolls continuously across the top of a financial news page, running for as long as the page is open, with no pause control. Does this meet WCAG 2.2.2?

options.text: Yes — scrolling text is exempt from 2.2.2 as long as it's informational
No — it starts automatically, runs well past 5 seconds, and is presented alongside other page content, with no pause, stop or hide mechanism available
Yes, because financial data needs to update continuously for accuracy

hints: There's no exemption in 2.2.2 for content being informational rather than decorative — the criterion is about motion competing with the user's ability to focus, regardless of the content's purpose.
Needing fresh data and needing it to scroll continuously with zero user control are two different requirements — the first doesn't require the second.
explanation: This fails 2.2.2. Being informational doesn't exempt content from the criterion — a continuously scrolling ticker meets all three conditions (auto-starts, runs indefinitely past 5 seconds, sits alongside other content someone might be reading) regardless of what the content is about. The need for current financial data justifies periodic updates, not the absence of any pause/stop/hide control — a user can be given a way to pause the ticker in place and still see accurate data whenever they choose to look at it.

prompt: Sort each finding into 'WCAG 2.2.2 (motion)' or 'WCAG 1.4.2 (audio).'

items.text: A background video loops silently and continuously with no pause control
A podcast episode begins playing automatically at full volume the moment the page loads, with no visible stop control
A ticker of scrolling headlines runs indefinitely alongside the main article text
An autoplaying video's soundtrack plays for 8 seconds with no way to mute it independent of the system volume

hints: Ask whether the finding is about something moving that competes for visual attention, or something making sound that competes with a screen reader.
A silent looping video is purely a motion concern; the same video with sound adds a separate audio concern on top.
explanation: Silent, continuously moving content — a muted looping video, a scrolling ticker — falls under 2.2.2's pause/stop/hide requirement, which is about visual motion competing for attention and reading time. Anything producing sound automatically for more than 3 seconds without a way to mute or stop it independent of system volume falls under 1.4.2, which is specifically about audio competing with a screen reader's own speech output. A single autoplaying video with sound can trigger both criteria at once, each needing its own fix.

prompt: An animated loading icon pulses at a measured rate of 2.5 times per second, in a muted blue color, covering a small area of the screen. Does it pass WCAG 2.3.1's general flash threshold?

options.text: Yes — it's below the 3-flashes-per-second threshold
No — any animated icon automatically fails 2.3.1
It can't be evaluated without knowing the exact pixel dimensions of the icon

hints: Compare the measured rate directly to the threshold from this lesson.
2.3.1 is about the flash rate and the area/contrast of the flashing region — a small, muted, sub-threshold-rate icon is exactly the kind of content the criterion was written to permit.
explanation: At 2.5 flashes per second, this icon is below the 3-per-second general threshold, and passes outright on rate alone. 2.3.1 doesn't fail all animation — it targets rapid, high-contrast flashing specifically, and content below the threshold rate doesn't need to separately clear the fuller general flash and red flash area tests. This is the kind of low-risk motion the criterion is specifically designed to leave alone.

prompt: A marketing team wants a countdown timer's final ten seconds to 'flash urgently' in bright red to drive conversions, alternating red and white roughly 4 times per second. Write the finding you'd give them before this ships.
hints: Two separate problems stack here: the rate is already above the general 3-per-second threshold, and the color is saturated red, which carries its own stricter threshold.
State the finding in terms of actual measured risk, not just 'this looks risky' — and offer a specific, still-urgent-feeling alternative.
explanation: A strong finding: *The proposed red/white alternation at roughly 4 times per second exceeds WCAG 2.3.1's general 3-flashes-per-second threshold, and because the color is saturated red, it's also subject to the stricter red flash threshold independently — this design needs to pass both to ship at all, and at this rate and color it's very unlikely to. This is a real photosensitive-seizure risk, not a stylistic concern.* Recommend: a genuinely urgent-feeling alternative that doesn't flash — a steady red background with a numerically counting-down digit, or a single smooth color transition rather than repeated alternation — achieves the same attention-grabbing goal without crossing either threshold.

prompt: An audit report states 'Video X: PASS (captions present)' based on confirming a .vtt caption file is attached and loads correctly in the player, without watching the video with captions on. True or false: this is sufficient evidence to mark the video compliant with WCAG 1.2.2.

config.statement: Confirming a caption file exists and loads is sufficient to mark a video 1.2.2-compliant, without checking what the captions actually say.
config.rubric: A full answer states that 1.2.2 requires captions to actually convey the audio content, and that a genuine check requires watching with captions on and audio off, not just confirming a file loads.

hints: This is the exact gap the lesson opened with — a file existing and a file being accurate are two different claims.
What would actually reveal whether 'diabetes' was transcribed as 'diet beat is'? Not a file-loads check.
explanation: False. A caption file loading correctly confirms only that a technical integration works, not that the captions accurately represent the audio. The only way to actually verify 1.2.2 compliance is watching the video with captions on and the audio off (or muted), checking the captions against what's actually being said — particularly through any specialised or technical vocabulary an auto-caption engine is likely to mishear. A 'PASS' based only on file presence is exactly the compliance-dashboard trap this lesson names directly.

prompt: A training video's transcript accurately records every word spoken. At one point, an alarm sounds in the background for several seconds while the presenter keeps talking, unaddressed by the transcript. Is the transcript complete?

options.text: Yes — every spoken word is present, which is the whole requirement
No — a complete transcript notes significant non-speech audio like an alarm in a bracketed description, since a hearing viewer perceives it even though nobody addresses it out loud
Yes, since the alarm isn't part of the dialogue and transcripts only cover speech

hints: Ask what a hearing viewer experiences at that moment that a transcript reader currently has no way to know about.
Non-speech audio only needs noting when it carries real meaning — an alarm sounding during a presentation clearly does.
explanation: The transcript is incomplete. A hearing viewer hears the alarm and experiences that moment differently than a silent one — possibly wondering, as the presenter apparently doesn't react, whether it's relevant. A transcript reader gets none of that unless it's noted, something like '[alarm sounds in background, continues for several seconds, unaddressed by presenter].' Significant non-speech audio is part of what a transcript owes whenever it carries real information or context, not only the literal words spoken.

prompt: Sort each dashboard change into 'genuinely reduces cumulative sensory load' or 'looks calmer but doesn't reduce the actual load.'

categories: Looks calmer but doesn't reduce the actual load

items.text: Reserving one consistent color to mean 'needs attention,' used nowhere else
Stripping all color from every tile and relying on text labels alone to distinguish them
items.category: Looks calmer but doesn't reduce the actual load

items.text: Limiting animation to a single element that genuinely needs attention right now, instead of several pulsing simultaneously
Reducing every tile's font size and padding to fit more on one screen 'to reduce scrolling'
items.category: Looks calmer but doesn't reduce the actual load

hints: The genuine reductions give a specific signal (color, motion) a real, consistent meaning rather than removing the signal entirely.
Both false options optimise for a different metric — visual minimalism, less scrolling — while making the actual parsing task harder.
explanation: The genuine reductions make color and motion mean something specific and consistent, so a glance actually tells the viewer something. Stripping color entirely removes a fast differentiator and replaces it with nothing, forcing individual label-reading instead. Shrinking everything to fit more on one screen optimises for less scrolling while adding real visual density and reading effort per element — a different metric than the one that actually matters, the same trap the earlier module named for click count versus cognitive load.

prompt: A support-ticket dashboard shows every ticket row with a badge, in one of six colors, none of them explained anywhere in the interface. Write the finding.
hints: Ask what a viewer can actually learn from the badges as they currently exist — can they tell what any given color means without hovering or guessing?
This is a cumulative/use-of-color style finding — think about whether there's a clean citation or whether it belongs as an evaluative finding.
explanation: A strong finding: *Every ticket row displays a colored badge (one of six colors observed: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, gray) with no visible legend, label, or tooltip anywhere in the interface explaining what any color means. A new or infrequent user has no way to determine priority, status, or urgency from the badge alone — the color is carrying real information with no way to decode it. This isn't cleanly a WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color violation (that criterion is about color being the only distinguisher between otherwise-identical states, not about undocumented color meaning), but it's a genuine barrier worth naming as an evaluative finding: color without a key is not information, it's noise with a hidden decoder ring.* Recommend: a visible legend, or better, replacing at least some colors with a short text label directly on the badge (e.g. 'Urgent' rather than just red), so the badge means something without requiring the color to be memorized or guessed.

prompt: A page has a decorative background video (no sound, purely visual texture) that loops continuously behind the hero text, with no pause control. Which criterion does this fail?

options.text: WCAG 1.4.2 Audio Control — the video needs a mute button
WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide — it auto-starts, runs well past 5 seconds, and sits alongside other content with no way to pause it
Nothing — decorative background video is always exempt from motion criteria

hints: There's no sound here, so the audio criterion doesn't apply — focus on the motion itself.
Purely decorative doesn't mean exempt — 2.2.2 doesn't have an exception for decorative content.
explanation: With no sound, 1.4.2 isn't in play — the finding is purely about motion. The video auto-starts, loops indefinitely (well past 5 seconds), and is presented alongside the hero text and other page content, meeting all three conditions that trigger WCAG 2.2.2's requirement for a pause, stop, or hide mechanism. 'Decorative' doesn't create an exemption in the criterion's text — the requirement is about the motion's behaviour, not its purpose.

prompt: A drag-and-drop task-board interface animates the dragged card following the user's cursor in real time. True or false: this motion needs to be disable-able under WCAG 2.3.3.

config.statement: The card-following-cursor animation in a drag-and-drop interaction needs to be disable-able under 2.3.3.
config.rubric: A full answer identifies this as essential motion — the interaction doesn't make sense without the card visibly following the cursor — which is exactly the narrow exception 2.3.3 carves out.

hints: Ask whether the drag-and-drop interaction would still function, or even make sense, without this specific motion.
This is the narrow 'essential' exception the lesson named directly — a dragged element needs to visibly move.
explanation: False. This is essential motion — a drag-and-drop interaction is meaningless without the dragged element visibly tracking the cursor; removing that motion wouldn't create a calmer version of the same interaction, it would break the interaction entirely. This is exactly the narrow case 2.3.3's essential exception exists for, distinct from the decorative parallax and slide-in effects covered earlier in this module that have no functional purpose at all.

prompt: Put these steps in order for reviewing a video's captions for real accuracy, not just presence.

items: Confirm a caption file exists and loads correctly in the player
Turn the audio off (or mute it) and watch the video with captions on only
Pay particular attention to technical, medical, or domain-specific terms most likely to be mistranscribed
Log any inaccuracy that changes or obscures meaning as a real finding, not a minor typo

hints: File presence is a fast first check, but it's the least informative step — it should come first because it's cheap, not because it's sufficient.
The step that actually reveals accuracy problems requires watching with sound off, not just confirming the file loads.
explanation: Confirming the file exists is fast and worth doing first, but it only rules out the most basic failure (no captions at all) — it says nothing about accuracy. The real test is watching with audio off and captions on, specifically attending to domain-specific vocabulary an auto-caption model is statistically likely to mishear. Logging inaccuracies that actually change meaning (versus a harmless typo) is what turns the check into a genuine finding rather than a pass/fail on file existence alone.

prompt: A promotional banner alternates between two shades of blue, roughly 5 times per second, covering about 15% of the viewport. What's the correct next step?

options.text: Automatically pass it, since blue isn't red and red is the only risky color

Measure it against the full general flash threshold (rate, area, and contrast between states) — 5 times per second is already above the 3-per-second baseline, so it needs the fuller test even though the color isn't red
Automatically fail it — any flashing above 3 per second fails outright regardless of further testing

hints: The red flash threshold is stricter than the general one, but the general threshold still applies to every other color — blue isn't exempt just for not being red.
Above 3 flashes per second, content isn't automatically failed — it needs the fuller general flash test (which also weighs area and contrast), it just isn't automatically safe either.
explanation: Blue isn't subject to the stricter red flash threshold, but it's still fully subject to the general flash threshold — and at roughly 5 times per second, this banner is already above the 3-per-second baseline that triggers the need for the fuller test (which also considers the flashing area and the contrast between the two states). The correct next step is running that fuller test, not assuming safety because the color isn't red, and not assuming automatic failure without checking area and contrast.

prompt: A webinar recording has accurate, human-reviewed captions, but the transcript provided separately for download is just the raw auto-generated file, full of errors, never corrected to match the reviewed captions. Write the finding.
hints: Two artifacts exist here — captions and a downloadable transcript — and only one of them was actually reviewed.
Someone who prefers reading a transcript over watching a video with captions is relying entirely on the uncorrected version.
explanation: A strong finding: *The video's burned-in/track captions were human-reviewed and are accurate, but the separately downloadable transcript is the original, unedited auto-generated output and contains the same errors the captions have already been corrected for. Anyone who prefers a standalone transcript — a common accommodation in its own right, not just a captions substitute — is relying entirely on the uncorrected version, with no indication anywhere that the two documents disagree.* Recommend: replace the downloadable transcript with the same reviewed text used for the captions, or clearly flag it as auto-generated and unverified if a reviewed version genuinely isn't available yet — the two shouldn't silently diverge with no visible warning.
