prompt: A dashboard redesign adds a single, consistent red badge that only appears on items genuinely needing urgent action, replacing a previous design where every item had a badge in one of six unexplained colors. True or false: this is a genuine reduction in cumulative sensory load.

config.statement: Replacing six unexplained badge colors with one consistent, meaningful badge that only appears when action is genuinely needed is a real reduction in sensory load.
config.rubric: A full answer notes that this both reduces the number of simultaneous signals and makes the remaining one carry real, decodable meaning — the two properties this lesson identified as genuine reductions.

hints: Compare this to the module's synthesis: genuine reductions give a signal real, consistent meaning and reduce how many things compete for attention at once.
This change does both — fewer visible badges overall, and the one that remains actually means something specific.
explanation: True. This does two things the lesson identified as genuine reductions at once: it cuts the number of simultaneously-present signals (badges only appear when truly needed, instead of on every item by default) and it gives the remaining signal a single, consistent, decodable meaning instead of six unexplained colors. This is different from the false 'reductions' earlier in the lesson (stripping all color, cramming more onto one screen) because it doesn't remove a real signal or add new density — it makes the signal that remains actually mean something.

prompt: Match each finding to the criterion or threshold it's actually tested against.

pairs.left: A video autoplays with sound for 6 seconds with no mute control independent of system volume
pairs.right: WCAG 1.4.2 Audio Control

pairs.left: A promotional element alternates saturated red and white 4 times per second
pairs.right: WCAG 2.3.1 red flash threshold

pairs.left: A silent hero carousel auto-advances every 4 seconds indefinitely, alongside page content, no pause control
pairs.right: WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide

pairs.left: A scroll-triggered slide-in effect has no function beyond visual style and no way to turn it off
pairs.right: WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions

hints: Sound past 3 seconds with no independent mute control is always the audio criterion.
Saturated red flashing specifically routes to the stricter red flash threshold, not just the general one.
explanation: Each finding maps to the criterion actually testing the specific mechanism at play: sound competing with a screen reader routes to 1.4.2; saturated red flashing routes to the stricter red flash threshold under 2.3.1; auto-advancing motion running alongside other content routes to 2.2.2's pause/stop/hide requirement; and non-essential, interaction-triggered motion with no disable mechanism routes to 2.3.3. Naming the right criterion for each is what turns a general complaint about 'too much movement' into four specific, individually fixable findings.

prompt: A news homepage has: an auto-advancing top-story carousel, three simultaneously auto-playing muted video thumbnails, a live-updating 'breaking news' ticker, and a notification bell that pulses continuously. None of these individually breaks a specific pause/stop rule badly enough to be an obvious single fix. Write the finding that captures the page as a whole.
hints: This is a cumulative-load finding, not four separate single-element findings — name the pattern, not just the pieces.
State honestly whether a clean citation covers the whole thing, or whether it's an evaluative finding, and say why it still belongs in the report.
explanation: A strong finding: *Four independently-moving elements are active simultaneously on first page load: an auto-advancing carousel, three auto-playing muted video previews, a continuously scrolling ticker, and a pulsing notification icon. Individually, each may or may not cleanly fail a specific WCAG motion criterion depending on its exact timing and pause controls — but together, the page presents four separate ongoing motion sources competing for attention at once, which is a real barrier for anyone with motion sensitivity or attention difficulty regardless of whether any single element is individually cited. This is logged as an evaluative cumulative-load finding, not tied to one WCAG number, because no single criterion measures simultaneous competing motion as a pattern — the same honest-limits approach used elsewhere in this track for barriers WCAG covers thinly.* Recommend: limit simultaneous auto-motion to at most one element at a time, with the rest activating only on direct user interaction.

prompt: In the appointment-booking flow from this lesson, four of the six form fields on the details screen already exist on the user's profile (name, date of birth, phone number, insurance ID). What's the correct classification of those four fields?

options.text: Essential — every form field is a necessary part of the task

Avoidable overhead — the system already has this information, so re-asking for it adds steps without gathering anything new (this is the same pattern as WCAG 3.3.7 Redundant Entry from an earlier module, applied at the level of a whole flow)
Essential, because forms should always be filled out completely from scratch

hints: Ask what new information each field actually collects — if the answer already exists in the system, the field isn't collecting anything new.
This is the same underlying pattern as an earlier module's redundant-entry finding, just applied to counting interactions instead of naming a WCAG criterion.
explanation: These four fields are avoidable overhead — the system already has this information on the user's profile, so displaying blank fields and asking for it again adds real taps and real cognitive effort while gathering nothing new. This is the interaction-counting version of the redundant-entry pattern from the cognitive-accessibility module: the fix there was auto-populating or offering to reuse an earlier value, and the fix here is exactly the same, just counted as taps saved rather than cited as a WCAG criterion.

prompt: A six-step flow and a fourteen-step flow with eight steps of overhead removed both end up being counted as 'six steps.' True or false: these two flows are equally good, since they have the same final count.

config.statement: A naturally six-step flow and a fourteen-step flow trimmed down to six steps are equally good, since the final counts match.
config.rubric: A full answer notes that once the honest minimum is actually reached — with nothing essential cut and no remaining avoidable overhead — the two flows genuinely are equivalent for the user, regardless of how each one got there; the caution is only about assuming a count is already minimal without checking, not about the trimmed flow being somehow inferior.

hints: Consider what actually matters to the person completing the task: the history of how the flow was built, or what it currently requires of them.
This isn't the same as saying 'any six-step count is fine' — it's specifically about a flow that's been checked and genuinely has no more overhead left to cut.
explanation: True, with the important condition already built into the premise: once the trimmed flow has actually reached its honest minimum (nothing essential cut, no avoidable overhead remaining), it presents the same real cost to the user as a flow that happened to need only six steps from the start — the person filling it out experiences six steps either way, with no memory of or exposure to the version that used to be fourteen. The caution from this lesson isn't that trimmed flows are inferior; it's that a count alone (six steps, fourteen steps) tells you nothing about whether that number is already the honest minimum or still has real overhead hiding inside it, which is why the classification step, not just the count, is the actual finding.

prompt: A password-reset flow: open app → tap 'Forgot password' → enter email → tap 'Send reset link' → open a separate email app → find the email → tap the link → it opens a browser (not the app) → enter a new password → enter it again to confirm → tap 'Reset' → return to the app → log in again with the new password. Build a short interaction inventory and name the most significant avoidable overhead.
hints: Count the app-switching itself as real cost, not just the taps within one app.
Ask which step exists only because of how the flow was built, not because the task genuinely requires it.
explanation: A strong answer counts roughly 12 steps as built, several of which involve switching between three separate contexts (the app, an email client, a browser) — each switch has a real cost beyond the single tap it appears to be, since it requires finding and reopening a different application entirely. The most significant avoidable overhead is the forced return trip: after resetting the password in the browser, the flow drops the user back at a login screen requiring the new password to be typed a third time, rather than automatically signing them in immediately after a successful reset (which the system could do, since it already has the new, just-set credential). That one change — auto-login immediately after reset — removes an entire redundant final step without weakening the reset flow's actual security.

prompt: A team argues that since their session-timeout warning already meets WCAG 2.2.1 (warn, extend 10x), adding autosave would be redundant engineering effort. What's the strongest response?

options.text: They're right — once 2.2.1 is met, no further protection is needed

2.2.1 compliance and actual data protection are different outcomes — the warn-and-extend mechanism still depends on the user being present and able to respond, which an involuntary, unpredictable interruption doesn't guarantee, so autosave closes a real remaining gap rather than duplicating existing protection
They're right, but only because autosave is always too expensive to build

hints: Being correct about the citation and being correct about the user's actual protection are two different claims — check whether this response conflates them.
Think specifically about what a warn-and-extend mechanism requires of the user in the moment, versus what autosave requires.
explanation: The team is factually right that 2.2.1 is met, and wrong that this settles the question. A warn-and-extend mechanism, however generous the extension, still depends entirely on the person being present and responsive at the moment the warning fires — a dependency an involuntary, unpredictable-length interruption specifically breaks. Autosave doesn't duplicate that protection; it closes the exact gap the warn-and-extend mechanism structurally can't reach, which is why it's worth recommending as a genuinely separate, non-redundant improvement rather than optional polish on top of already-sufficient compliance.

prompt: A team decides the fix for the timeout problem is simply extending the warning-triggered grace period from 150 minutes to 24 hours. True or false: this fully closes the gap identified in this lesson.

config.statement: Extending the grace period to 24 hours fully closes the gap between WCAG 2.2.1 compliance and actually protecting an unpredictable interruption.
config.rubric: A full answer identifies that the mechanism still requires the user to see and respond to the warning at the moment it fires — a longer grace period afterward doesn't change that upstream dependency.

hints: The gap identified in this lesson is about the moment the warning appears and needs a response, not about how long the resulting grace period lasts.
Ask: does a bigger number change what the user has to do at the exact moment they're mid-episode?
explanation: False. However long the resulting grace period is, the mechanism still requires the person to see the warning dialog and respond to it at the moment it appears — and that's exactly the moment an involuntary episode may make impossible. The fix that actually closes the gap removes the dependency on an in-the-moment response entirely, which is what autosave does and a longer extension window, however generous, does not.

prompt: Which framing of a redone-work finding is the stronger, more accurate claim?

options.text: "This wastes the user's time and should be fixed for a better experience"
"For a user with a fixed daily energy budget, losing this work isn't a 40-minute delay — it can mean the task doesn't get completed today, or this week, at all"
"Users don't like retyping information"

hints: The stronger claim is specific about the actual consequence for someone whose capacity is a hard limit, not a preference.
"Wastes time" and "a task may not get completed at all" are different magnitudes of consequence — which one is actually true here?
explanation: The strongest framing states the real, specific consequence: for someone whose energy on a given day is a hard limit rather than a preference, losing forty minutes of work isn't merely lost time that can be made up later — it can directly mean the task doesn't get finished today, this week, or possibly at all if the underlying condition varies unpredictably. 'Wastes time' and 'users don't like it' both understate this into a generic UX complaint, losing the actual argument that makes this a genuine accessibility finding rather than a nice-to-have.

prompt: A five-page job application saves nothing until the final page is submitted. Write the finding, including the specific consequence for a user with a limited daily energy budget.
hints: Name what a failure at page 4 would cost specifically — all four completed pages, not just the current one.
State the consequence in terms of task completion, not just time — that's the distinction this lesson is built around.
explanation: A strong finding: *This five-page application saves nothing to the server until the final page is submitted — a crash, closed tab, or session timeout at any point before submission, including on page 4 after three full pages of careful work, costs the entire application equally, regardless of how much was actually completed. For a user whose available energy on a given day is a fixed, non-renewable budget, this isn't a time-loss problem: a failure this late may mean the application doesn't get finished today, and depending on the underlying condition, possibly not this week — a genuinely different and more serious outcome than 'has to redo forty minutes of typing.'* Recommend: save each page's answers to the server as soon as the user moves past it, so a later failure costs at most the current, unsaved page rather than the entire application.

prompt: Match each saving strategy to what a failure would cost under it.

pairs.left: No saving until final submission on a 5-page form
pairs.right: All 5 pages of work, regardless of how much was completed

pairs.left: Saving committed on each 'Next' page transition
pairs.right: At most the current, still-in-progress page

pairs.left: Saving committed per individual field as it's completed
pairs.right: At most the last few unsaved fields on the current page

pairs.left: Continuous autosave to a draft as the user types, independent of any timer
pairs.right: Effectively nothing, regardless of session length or interruption timing

hints: Each strategy bounds the maximum possible loss at a smaller and smaller unit of work, from 'the whole form' down to 'essentially nothing.'
The finer-grained the saving unit (whole form vs. page vs. field vs. continuous), the smaller the worst-case loss.
explanation: Each row is a strictly smaller worst-case loss than the one above it, because each strategy saves at a finer unit of work. No saving at all makes the entire form an all-or-nothing bet on getting all the way to the end without interruption. Per-page saving bounds the loss to the current page. Per-field saving bounds it further, to whatever hasn't been committed yet on the current page. Continuous autosave, independent of any timer or transition event, approaches zero loss regardless of when or how long an interruption lasts — which is exactly the property an unpredictable-duration interruption requires.

prompt: A photo-editing app requires a two-finger pinch gesture to crop an image, with no alternative control. What's the accurate framing of this barrier?

options.text: It's a minor inconvenience for anyone without two free hands, but not a real accessibility barrier
It silently assumes two functioning hands are available to perform the gesture, with no single-hand or keyboard/button-based alternative offered for anyone who can't
Pinch gestures are always accessible on modern touchscreens regardless of how many hands are available

hints: Ask specifically what physical resources this gesture requires that a single-hand-operable alternative wouldn't.
Two-finger gestures performed by one hand are possible for some users and genuinely not possible for others — the question is whether any alternative exists at all.
explanation: A two-finger pinch with no alternative silently assumes the user has two functioning hands, or at minimum full dexterity in one hand to perform a two-point gesture unaided — an assumption that fails for anyone missing that capacity, whether from a permanent condition, a temporary injury, or an arm occupied holding the device itself or something else entirely (an IV line, a mobility aid, a child). This is a real, structural accessibility barrier, not a minor inconvenience, and the fix is an alternative single-tap or slider-based crop control that achieves the same result without requiring two simultaneous points of contact.

prompt: A team fixes the 'Log dose taken' button's reachability problem by making the button significantly larger, without moving its position from the top of the screen. True or false: this fully resolves the reachability finding from this lesson.

config.statement: Making the button larger, without changing its position, fully resolves the one-handed reachability problem.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes target size from reachability — a larger button is still unreachable if the thumb's range of motion in a lying-down posture can't physically get to that zone of the screen at all.

hints: This is the same size-versus-reachability distinction the lesson names directly — check whether size actually addresses the mechanism at play.
If a thumb genuinely can't stretch to the top of the screen while lying down, does making the target bigger at that same unreachable position help at all?
explanation: False. Size and reachability are two separate properties. A larger button at the same position doesn't help if a one-handed thumb, in a lying-down posture with reduced range of motion, still can't physically stretch to that zone of the screen at all — the problem was never that the button was too small to hit accurately once reached, it's that the position itself is outside a realistic reach zone for this posture. The actual fix is moving the primary action toward the bottom of the layout or into a persistent, always-reachable position, which is a placement change, not a size change.

prompt: An auditor, anticipating pushback, cites WCAG 2.2.1 as the formal basis for an energy-cost finding about redone work, even though 2.2.1 doesn't actually mention data loss or autosave anywhere in its text. True or false: this is a defensible way to strengthen the finding.

config.statement: Citing 2.2.1 as the formal basis for a redone-work finding, even though its text doesn't cover data loss or autosave, strengthens the finding.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that a citation stretched past what it actually says weakens the finding's credibility the moment a careful reader checks it, and that the honest evaluative framing (as modelled throughout this module) is the stronger, more defensible choice.

hints: Think about what happens to this finding, and every other finding in the same audit, once a reviewer who knows 2.2.1's actual text checks the citation and finds it doesn't say what's being claimed.
This is the exact mistake the lesson names as the second of two ways to get this wrong.
explanation: False. Stretching 2.2.1 to cover something its text doesn't actually address is the second of the two mistakes this lesson names directly — it hands a careful reviewer an easy, legitimate reason to dismiss the finding the moment they check the citation against what it actually says, and that damage doesn't stay contained to one finding; it makes every other citation in the same audit look less trustworthy too. The stronger, more defensible move is exactly what this module has modelled throughout: name the finding as evaluative, back it with a precise count and a specific consequence, and cite 2.2.1 only for what it genuinely does say (timing must be adjustable) as supporting context, not as the whole justification.

prompt: Rewrite this finding to survive 'that's not WCAG': 'The checkout flow has too many steps and could be more energy-efficient for disabled users.'
hints: Add the actual number and the specific breakdown of which steps are avoidable.
State the real consequence, not a general claim about efficiency.
Be explicit about which part of the finding is formal WCAG conformance and which part is evaluative judgment.
explanation: A strong rewrite: *The checkout flow requires 11 discrete steps as built. Of these, 4 are avoidable: a shipping-method screen with a single available option (no real choice being made), a duplicate email-confirmation field re-asking for an address already entered two fields earlier (the same redundant-entry pattern named elsewhere in this track), and a second 'Are you sure?' confirmation on top of an already-explicit 'Place order' button. A defensible minimum is 7 steps. For a user managing a limited, non-renewable daily energy budget, four extra steps aren't a minor inconvenience — on a bad day, they can be the difference between completing a purchase and abandoning it partway through with no clear way to resume later. This finding sits outside formal WCAG conformance scope (there's no numbered criterion for interaction count); it's an evaluative finding grounded in a specific, checkable count, offered with the same standing as the audit's cited findings, not less. Recommend: remove the single-option selector, auto-populate the duplicate email field, and collapse the two confirmations into one.* This version replaces impression with a checkable number, names the specific steps, states the real consequence, and is explicit about its own evidentiary status rather than either dropping the point or overclaiming a citation.

prompt: A recurring bill-pay flow asks the user to re-select their payment method from a list every single month, even though 95% of users always pick the same saved card. What's the most accurate classification of this step?

options.text: Essential — payment method should always be actively reconfirmed

Avoidable overhead for the vast majority of users — the system could default to the most-recently-used method with a single, low-effort way to change it, rather than forcing an active reselection every time
This isn't a real interaction cost issue since it's only one tap

hints: One tap repeated every single month, for a choice that's almost always the same, still adds up as real, avoidable overhead.
The fix isn't removing the choice entirely, it's changing the default so the choice only requires action when someone actually wants to change it.
explanation: This is avoidable overhead for the large majority of users, even though it's 'only' one tap — the interaction-counting method treats every repeated, low-information step as real cost, not just steps that individually feel large. The fix isn't removing the ability to choose a payment method (a genuine, sometimes-needed choice for the remaining users), it's defaulting to the most recently used method with an easy, visible way to change it, so the step only costs anything for the person who actually wants to make a different choice this time.

prompt: Sort each mitigation into 'genuinely prevents data loss' or 'only reduces how often loss happens.'

categories: Only reduces how often loss happens

items.text: Continuous autosave to a draft as the user types
Extending a fixed session timeout from 15 to 30 minutes
items.category: Only reduces how often loss happens

items.text: Saving each page's data to the server the moment 'Next' is tapped
Adding a warning dialog at 90% of the time limit, with no autosave behind it
items.category: Only reduces how often loss happens

hints: Ask whether each mitigation removes the possibility of loss, or just shrinks the window in which it can happen.
A warning with nothing behind it, and a longer (but still fixed) timeout, both still lose everything the moment they're missed or exceeded.
explanation: Autosave and per-page saving both genuinely prevent loss because they commit real data independent of whether the user is present, attentive, or within an arbitrary time window — there's no remaining scenario in which the saved portion is lost. A longer fixed timeout and a warning with no autosave behind it both still lose everything the moment they're exceeded or missed respectively; they shrink the odds for people who happen to fit inside the new number or notice the warning, without removing the underlying risk for anyone who doesn't.

prompt: A meal-delivery app's 'reorder your last order' feature requires: open app, tap 'Orders,' find the order in a long history list (no search), tap it, tap 'Reorder,' review each item individually with a separate 'confirm this item' tap per item (an 8-item order needs 8 of these), then tap 'Checkout.' Count the interactions and name the single biggest reduction.
hints: The per-item confirmation is the step that scales badly — its cost grows with order size in a way nothing else in the flow does.
Ask what information a per-item confirm is actually gathering, given the user already tapped 'Reorder' on the whole order.
explanation: As built, this is roughly 5 fixed steps plus one confirmation tap per item — 13 total for an 8-item order, and it gets worse for anyone who orders more. The single biggest reduction is removing the per-item confirmation entirely: tapping 'Reorder' on a specific past order already signals a clear intent to reorder everything in it, and the confirmation step gathers no new information the system doesn't already have — it just charges a linear, order-size-scaling tax on a decision the user already made once. A single review-and-edit screen showing the whole reordered cart, with the ability to remove any one item, achieves the same safety (nothing gets ordered by accident) without the per-item repetition.

prompt: A telehealth intake form times out after 10 minutes with a warning-and-extend mechanism that fully satisfies WCAG 2.2.1, and has no autosave. True or false: for a patient whose appointment reason is an acute symptom flare that could itself interrupt form-filling at any moment, this is adequately protective.

config.statement: A compliant warning-and-extend mechanism, with no autosave, is adequately protective for a patient whose own symptoms might interrupt the form at any unpredictable moment.
config.rubric: A full answer applies this module's central distinction directly: 2.2.1 compliance and actual protection against an involuntary, unpredictable interruption are different claims, and this scenario is precisely the case autosave is needed for.

hints: This scenario is the direct, real-world case this module's second lesson is built around — apply that reasoning here specifically.
The patient's own reason for the appointment is itself a plausible source of an unpredictable mid-form interruption.
explanation: False. This is precisely the situation where the gap between WCAG compliance and actual protection matters most: a patient filling out an intake form because of an acute symptom is at real, elevated risk of exactly the kind of involuntary, unpredictable-length interruption a warn-and-extend mechanism can't reach, since it depends on the person being present and able to respond to a dialog. Autosave is the mechanism that actually protects this specific patient's typed answers regardless of what happens or how long it lasts — and the acute nature of the appointment itself makes this a higher-stakes case for that gap, not a lower one.

prompt: A settings screen requires a double-tap-and-hold gesture (tap twice quickly, then hold on the second tap) to unlock a 'delete all data' option, explained as a deliberate friction to prevent accidental deletion. Is this gesture defensible under a one-handed-use review?

options.text: No — any gesture more complex than a single tap automatically fails a one-handed review

It's a genuine, deliberate trade-off (friction to prevent an irreversible, destructive action) worth naming as such, but the specific gesture chosen should still be checked for whether it's completable one-handed (a double-tap-and-hold is, a two-finger gesture would not be) rather than assumed either safe or unsafe by default
Yes — any friction on a destructive action is automatically justified regardless of what the gesture actually requires physically

hints: This is the same pattern as the paste-blocking and vague-login-error caveats from earlier modules — a deliberate trade-off deserves to be evaluated on its own specific terms, not waved through or rejected by default.
A double-tap-and-hold, unlike a two-finger pinch, can be performed by a single thumb — check the actual mechanical requirement, not just whether friction exists.
explanation: Deliberate friction on an irreversible, destructive action is a legitimate design goal, echoing the paste-blocking and vague-login-error trade-offs named in earlier modules — it shouldn't be dismissed just because it adds steps. But 'friction is justified' doesn't mean any gesture is automatically fine; the actual physical requirement still needs checking. A double-tap-and-hold, performed by a single thumb in sequence, is genuinely completable one-handed. A two-finger gesture chosen for the same purpose would not be, and would need to be flagged and replaced with a single-hand-completable alternative that still provides the intended friction (a confirmation step, a typed 'DELETE' phrase) rather than one relying on two simultaneous points of contact.

prompt: Put these steps in order for auditing a task's redo-risk, from fastest/cheapest check to most thorough.

items: Check whether the flow has any saving mechanism at all before a final submission
Deliberately close the tab or lose connection partway through, and observe exactly what's lost on return
Identify the smallest unit of work a failure at each stage would actually cost
Write the specific consequence for a user whose available energy today is a fixed, non-renewable budget

hints: The fastest check is just looking for the presence of any intermediate saving at all, before testing anything.
The consequence framing comes last because it depends on already knowing exactly what would be lost and at what stage.
explanation: Checking for any intermediate saving mechanism at all is the fastest, cheapest first pass — it immediately flags flows with no protection whatsoever. Actually testing by deliberately triggering a failure is what turns an assumption into an observed fact, the same 'test it, don't guess' standard from the earlier cognitive-load module's lab. Identifying the smallest unit of loss at each stage turns that observation into a structured finding. And the energy-budget consequence framing comes last because it depends on already knowing precisely what would be lost and when — it's the argument that makes the finding land, built on top of the evidence gathered in the first three steps.

prompt: A hospital patient-portal app's 'Message your care team' feature requires holding down a microphone icon continuously while speaking a voice message (release ends recording), with no text-input alternative. Write the finding.
hints: This combines two things from this module: a sustained-hold gesture requiring a steady hand, and the total absence of any alternative input method.
State the specific population this excludes and propose a concrete, buildable fix.
explanation: A strong finding: *The only way to message a care team is a press-and-hold voice recording control with no text-input alternative anywhere in the flow. This requires continuous, steady contact for the full duration of the message, which is difficult or impossible for anyone with a tremor, anyone who can't speak clearly or at all in the moment (a common state during or after a health crisis), and anyone who simply can't hold a device steady with one hand for an extended period while also speaking. There's no fallback of any kind — a user who can't complete this specific gesture in this specific way cannot message their care team through the app at all.* Recommend: add a standard text-input option alongside voice, and if voice input is retained, replace the sustained-hold with a tap-to-start/tap-to-stop recording pattern that doesn't require continuous physical contact for the message's full length.

prompt: A crisis-text-line app requires a mandatory dropdown ('How did you hear about us?') before showing the text-line number, with no skip option. Marketing attribution is a real, legitimate business need. Does that justify making this field mandatory here?

options.text: Yes — any legitimate business need justifies a mandatory field anywhere in the product

No — a legitimate long-term business need doesn't automatically justify blocking access to an urgent resource behind it; the immediate task (reaching a crisis number) doesn't require this information at all
It depends only on how short the dropdown's list of options is

hints: Marketing attribution being useful to the business is a different question from whether this specific task, right now, needs it.
Ask what happens to someone in genuine crisis who has to make a selection before reaching help.
explanation: A legitimate business need for marketing attribution data doesn't transfer into a justification for gating access to an urgent resource behind it — the two are separate questions. The task in front of this specific user (reaching a crisis line number) doesn't require attribution data at all, and blocking it behind a mandatory field imposes a real, serious cost on someone in an urgent situation for the sake of a business goal that could be served just as well by an optional, later, or even entirely separate mechanism (like tracking the referring link itself).

prompt: A domestic-violence support organisation's website has a mandatory field on its first page: 'What's your current living situation?' with a free-text box, before any resource or hotline number is shown. Write the finding and a specific fix.
hints: This is a heightened-stakes version of the crisis-app example — think specifically about the safety implications of a mandatory, undeletable disclosure at this exact moment.
The fix should let someone reach the resource first, and consider that browser history or a shared device could itself be a safety risk for typed content.
explanation: A strong finding: *The site requires a written description of the user's living situation before displaying any hotline number or resource — for a domestic-violence support site specifically, this is a serious compounding problem: it delays access to urgent help, and it requires typing potentially identifying, sensitive content on a device that may not be private or safe for the user to use, creating a real safety risk on top of the dignity cost already covered in this lesson.* Recommend: display the hotline number and immediate resources with zero required fields whatsoever — no login, no disclosure — and move any optional intake information to a separate, clearly optional step reachable only after the person has what they came for, with a clearly visible 'quick exit' mechanism given the safety stakes specific to this context.

prompt: A job application's photo-upload field has no stated purpose anywhere in the form or its documentation. True or false: the absence of any stated purpose is itself a stronger, more direct finding than a field whose stated purpose is real but over-broad (like the exact-date-of-birth example).

config.statement: A field with no stated purpose at all is a more direct finding than a field with a real but over-broad purpose.
config.rubric: A full answer notes that a field with zero articulable purpose fails the 'explain this to the person's face' test immediately and completely, while an over-broad field at least has a real purpose that just needs narrowing — different severities of the same underlying problem.

hints: One field has some legitimate purpose that's just collecting more than it needs to; the other has no stated purpose at all.
Which one fails the 'explain this to the person's face' test more completely?
explanation: True. A field with a real, if over-broad, stated purpose (verifying legal working age) at least survives part of the necessity test — it just needs narrowing to a threshold rather than an exact value. A field with no stated purpose at all fails the test completely and immediately: there's no explanation to narrow, because none exists. Both are real findings, but the second is the more direct case of 'this data is being collected because nobody questioned it, not because anyone decided it was needed' — exactly the 'just in case' pattern this lesson opened with.

prompt: A telehealth intake form asks about current medications, and every answer is visible to the full clinical team roster, including specialists the patient hasn't been referred to yet and administrative staff who schedule appointments. What's the correct fix?

options.text: Remove the medications question entirely, since any routing risk means it shouldn't be asked

Scope visibility to the clinicians actually treating this patient, rather than the full roster by default — administrative scheduling staff don't need clinical medication details to do their job, and unreferred specialists don't yet have a treating relationship with this patient
Nothing needs to change, since all staff are bound by general confidentiality policies

hints: The question itself is clinically legitimate and important — the problem, as in the lesson, is who can see the answer, not whether it should be asked.
Ask specifically what an administrative scheduler needs to see to do their actual job, versus what a treating clinician needs.
explanation: The medications question is clinically necessary and shouldn't be removed — the actual defect is visibility scoped to a full roster rather than the specific people with an active treating relationship to this patient. Administrative scheduling staff have no operational need for clinical medication details, and specialists the patient hasn't been referred to yet have no treating relationship justifying access either. 'Bound by confidentiality policy' is a behavioural expectation, not a technical control — the fix is a system that only shows this information to roles that structurally need it, not a policy asking everyone with access not to misuse it.

prompt: A five-person community nonprofit routes all accommodation requests to a single shared inbox checked by whichever of the two co-directors is available. True or false: this is automatically the same finding as the university's shared-desk-inbox example from this lesson.

config.statement: A five-person nonprofit's single shared inbox, checked by one of two co-directors, is automatically the same severity of finding as a large university routing sensitive requests to whoever covers a shared desk.
config.rubric: A full answer applies the lesson's honest caveat: the test is whether access is scoped as narrowly as the organisation's real structure allows, not whether it's perfectly scoped in the abstract — a small org with two trusted, senior people is a different, more defensible case than a large org routing to an undifferentiated shared desk.

hints: The lesson explicitly names a caveat about organisation size and real capacity — apply it here directly.
Compare who's actually receiving the disclosure in each case: two named co-directors, versus 'whoever happens to be covering a desk.'
explanation: False, and this is exactly the honest caveat the lesson names directly: the test is whether access is scoped as narrowly as the organisation's actual structure and staffing allow, not whether it matches an idealised, fully role-specific system. Two named, senior co-directors receiving sensitive requests at a five-person nonprofit is a meaningfully narrower and more defensible destination than an undifferentiated 'whoever's covering the desk today' at a large university with the staffing to build real role-based routing and simply hadn't. Same general shape of finding, genuinely different severity.

prompt: Sort each button/flow description into the specific dark-pattern name it matches, or 'not a dark pattern.'

items.text: A decline button reading 'No, I don't want to protect my family'
A subscription that can be started with one tap online but can only be cancelled by calling a phone line open 10am-2pm weekdays
A single retention offer with a neutrally-worded 'No thanks' button that, once clicked, immediately cancels
A decline button reading simply 'Continue cancelling'

hints: Confirmshaming is specifically about the wording used on the decline option, not the number of steps involved.
Roach motel is specifically about entry being easy and exit being disproportionately harder, not about wording.
explanation: 'No, I don't want to protect my family' loads the decline option with guilt-inducing language — confirmshaming. A subscription that's one tap to start and only cancellable through a narrow phone window is the classic asymmetry that defines roach motel — easy in, deliberately hard out. A single, honestly-worded retention offer with an immediate, respected decline isn't a dark pattern at all — one offer and a neutral decline button are ordinary, legitimate business behaviour. 'Continue cancelling' is exactly the neutral phrasing that avoids confirmshaming, stating the action plainly with no editorial framing.

prompt: You've fully documented a six-screen cancellation flow (two retention offers with confirmshamed decline buttons, a mandatory survey, then the real cancel button). Write the finding.
hints: Quote the actual copy, state the exact screen count, and name both patterns present by their specific names.
Include the fatigue-exploitation mechanism explicitly, not just a list of screens.
Propose a specific, concrete replacement flow, not a general note to 'simplify.'
explanation: A strong finding: *Cancelling a subscription requires six screens: a 50%-off retention offer with decline text reading "No thanks, I'll keep paying full price"; a second retention screen listing lost features with decline text reading "Continue cancelling"; a mandatory "Why are you leaving?" dropdown with no skip option; then the actual cancel button. This combines two named dark patterns — confirmshaming (loaded decline copy on screen one) and roach motel (six-screen exit versus one-tap entry). This structure doesn't just annoy users, it specifically exploits declining willingness to keep clicking through friction — for a user managing a limited daily energy budget, giving up and remaining subscribed isn't an edge case this flow accidentally produces, it's the outcome this specific structure is built to produce.* Recommend: a single-screen cancellation with one optional, neutrally-worded retention offer and an immediate, one-click 'Cancel subscription' option that doesn't require declining anything first.

prompt: Which rewrite of 'Your session has expired due to inactivity' (shown to a user who was continuously typing) is the most honest and defensible?

options.text: 'Your session has expired due to a technical error on our end' — stating a different specific cause instead
'Your session ended and your answers weren't saved. We're sorry.' — stating only what's actually verifiable, without inventing any specific cause
'You were inactive for too long — please try again' — restating the same claim in different words

hints: The problem with the original wasn't just that it named the wrong cause — it's that it confidently named any specific cause at all without being able to verify it in general.
The most defensible version doesn't guess at a replacement cause; it states only what's actually known.
explanation: The most honest rewrite states only what the system can actually verify — the session ended and the data wasn't saved — without asserting a specific cause it may not actually know in every case. Swapping in a different specific claim ('technical error on our end') is more honest about this particular bug but repeats the same underlying mistake for the next bug with a different cause. Restating the same false claim in different words doesn't fix anything at all. The version that survives is the one making the smallest, most defensible claim.

prompt: During a confirmed processor outage, a checkout page is changed to show 'Payment declined. Please check your card details and try again' for every transaction, identical to the message shown during normal card-specific declines. True or false: using the identical message in both cases is fine, since the underlying declined-payment fact is technically true in both.

config.statement: Using the identical 'please check your card details' message during a known systemic outage and during a genuine card-specific decline is fine, since a payment was declined in both cases.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes the fact of a decline (true in both cases) from the message's specific claimed cause (false during the outage), and explains the harm of repeatedly directing customers to fix information that was never wrong.

hints: The literal fact ('payment declined') being true doesn't make every possible explanation of why also true.
Think about what dozens of customers are being individually told to do, and whether that action could possibly fix a processor outage.
explanation: False. 'Payment declined' being technically true doesn't make 'please check your card details' true — during a confirmed outage, the decline has nothing to do with any customer's card details, and telling each person individually to re-check and re-enter correct information is asking them to perform an action that cannot possibly fix the actual problem, potentially several times each. The system knows, in this scenario, that an outage is occurring — using that known information to show an accurate message ('we're having trouble processing payments right now, this isn't about your card') is both more honest and prevents dozens of people independently blaming themselves for a shared systemic failure.

prompt: A team argues: 'Our benefits kiosk passed every WCAG check in the audit, so any further concerns about it are out of scope for an accessibility review.' True or false: this is a defensible position.

config.statement: Passing every WCAG conformance check means any further dignity-related concerns about the kiosk are out of scope for the review.
config.rubric: A full answer states that conformance and dignity are separate, both-real axes, and that a good audit reports both clearly labelled rather than treating a conformance pass as closing the whole question.

hints: This is the module's central distinction — apply it directly to the team's specific claim.
Ask whether 'passes conformance' and 'doesn't cause real harm' are actually the same claim.
explanation: False. Conformance and dignity are separate, both-real axes, and this lesson's kiosk example demonstrates exactly why — every individual conformance check can pass while the kiosk's physical placement and checkbox wording still force a stigmatised, public disclosure. A conformance pass answers a real but narrower question than 'does this treat the person using it with respect,' and a good audit reports both clearly, rather than treating a clean conformance scorecard as evidence the second question doesn't need asking.

prompt: A food-bank intake tablet, placed on an open counter with a line of people waiting behind the person using it, asks a mandatory question: 'Select your reason for needing assistance today' from a visible dropdown of options including 'unemployment,' 'domestic violence,' and 'addiction recovery.' Write the finding.
hints: This combines the physical-placement problem and the specific-wording problem from this lesson, in a genuinely high-stakes setting.
State the conformance status honestly, name the specific harm, and propose a concrete, buildable fix.
explanation: A strong finding: *The intake tablet is placed on an open counter with the current question visibly on-screen to anyone in the waiting line behind the user, including a dropdown listing sensitive categories like 'domestic violence' and 'addiction recovery' that a person must select in full view of others. This sits outside formal WCAG conformance scope — the tablet interface itself may be fully accessible and correctly built — but is a real, specific dignity harm: it forces a public, visible disclosure of a stigmatised personal circumstance to strangers in line, at the exact moment someone is already in a vulnerable position seeking help.* Recommend: a privacy screen or angled placement preventing the current screen from being visible to anyone but the user, and replacing the visible category dropdown with a private, single-tap or swipe interaction that doesn't display the selected category on a shared or visible screen — or moving this specific question to a private conversation with a caseworker rather than a public kiosk at all.

prompt: A rental application asks for the applicant's exact salary figure, explained as 'we need to verify you earn at least 3x the monthly rent.' What's the more privacy-respecting field that serves the identical stated purpose?

options.text: A yes/no confirmation: 'Do you earn at least 3x the monthly rent ($X,XXX/month)?' with proof required only if requested later
There's no way to verify this without the exact figure
Ask for the applicant's full annual tax return instead, to be thorough

hints: This is the same threshold-versus-exact-value pattern from the date-of-birth example — apply it here.
The stated purpose is a threshold check, so the field should ask about the threshold, not the exact number.
explanation: A threshold confirmation ('do you earn at least $X/month') verifies exactly what the stated purpose requires without exposing the applicant's precise salary to a landlord who doesn't need to know the exact figure, only whether it clears a specific bar. Requiring a full tax return goes drastically the other direction, requesting far more than even the exact-salary version would. 'No way to verify without the exact figure' isn't true — proof of income at the stated threshold (a pay stub, an offer letter) can be requested if needed, without the applicant disclosing the precise number as a mandatory first step.

prompt: A support-ticket system CCs a customer's full ticket history, including any mention of a disability accommodation, to every agent in a round-robin queue, so 'whoever picks it up next has full context.' True or false: this is a reasonable trade-off for continuity of service.

config.statement: CCing a customer's full history, including disability accommodation mentions, to every agent in a round-robin queue is a reasonable trade-off for service continuity.
config.rubric: A full answer notes that continuity can be achieved by making history visible to whichever agent is actually assigned the ticket, rather than broadcasting it to the entire queue in advance — the same narrow-routing principle from the lesson.

hints: Ask whether 'the assigned agent can see history' and 'every agent in the queue receives it in advance' are actually the same requirement.
Continuity needs the information available to whoever picks it up — it doesn't need the information sent to everyone who might.
explanation: False. Continuity of service requires that whichever agent is actually assigned a ticket can see its history — it doesn't require broadcasting that history to the entire queue in advance of assignment. A system where history is visible only once a ticket is claimed, rather than pushed out to every potential agent beforehand, achieves the identical continuity goal while exposing the disability accommodation mention to only the one agent who ends up actually handling it, not everyone who might have.

prompt: A gym membership can be cancelled online with one click, and doing so shows a plain confirmation: 'Your membership is cancelled effective [date]. We're sorry to see you go.' No retention offer, no survey, no additional screens. Is this a dark pattern?

options.text: Yes — any cancellation flow that doesn't attempt retention is automatically suspicious
No — a single-step, honestly-worded cancellation with no forced friction, loaded language, or blocking steps is exactly what a non-dark-pattern flow looks like
It depends on how many months the person had been a member

hints: Compare this directly to the roach-motel and confirmshaming examples from the lesson — what's actually missing here that made those cases dark patterns?
The absence of a retention attempt isn't itself suspicious — the presence of manipulative structure is what defines a dark pattern.
explanation: This is not a dark pattern — it's the honest baseline the lesson's examples were being measured against. No staged friction, no loaded language on any option, no mandatory blocking step between the request and the outcome. A company choosing not to attempt retention at all is a legitimate business choice, and its absence doesn't make a flow suspicious — what makes a flow a dark pattern is the presence of manipulative structure (confirmshaming copy, disproportionate exit friction), not the absence of a sales attempt.

prompt: An online grocery delivery app auto-enrols every new customer into a paid membership trial via a pre-checked checkbox at checkout, in small text below the main 'Place order' button, with no separate confirmation step. Write the finding, naming the specific pattern.
hints: This is forced continuity combined with a pre-checked opt-out pattern — name both explicitly.
State what a customer has to actively notice and undo to avoid being enrolled.
explanation: A strong finding: *A pre-checked checkbox enrolling the customer in a paid membership trial appears in small text below the main 'Place order' button, with no separate confirmation or highlighted callout. A customer completing an ordinary grocery order has to notice, read, and actively uncheck a small, easily-missed box to avoid being enrolled — the default state does the enrolling, and inattention (a single missed line of small text) does the rest. This is a pre-checked opt-out pattern feeding into forced continuity (the trial auto-converts to a paid subscription unless separately cancelled later). Recommend: the membership offer should require an active, deliberate opt-in — an unchecked box, or a separate clearly-labelled step — never a pre-checked default that inattention silently confirms.*

prompt: An error message reads 'Something went wrong. Please try again.' for a genuinely unknown server error. True or false: this message is a blame-language problem of the same kind as 'Your session expired due to inactivity.'

config.statement: 'Something went wrong, please try again' is the same kind of blame-language problem as a message that falsely claims the session expired due to inactivity.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes a message that's honestly vague about an unknown cause from one that confidently asserts a specific, false, user-implicating cause — the first is a clarity gap, the second is blame.

hints: One message claims to know a specific cause and gets it wrong; the other admits it doesn't know the cause at all.
Vagueness and false confident blame are different failures, even though both are imperfect messages.
explanation: False. 'Something went wrong, please try again' is honestly vague — it doesn't claim to know a specific cause, and critically, it doesn't attribute the failure to anything the user did. This is a clarity shortfall (it could certainly be more helpful) but not a blame problem. 'Your session expired due to inactivity' is worse in kind, not just degree: it confidently asserts a specific cause, that cause is false, and the false cause specifically implicates the user's own behaviour. The two failures aren't equivalent even though neither message is ideal.

prompt: Match each finding to whether it sits inside formal WCAG conformance scope or is a separate, evaluative dignity/energy-cost finding.

pairs.left: A form field lacks a programmatically associated label
pairs.right: Inside WCAG conformance scope (4.1.2)

pairs.left: A benefits kiosk with no privacy screen forces a stigmatised disclosure into public view
pairs.right: Outside formal conformance scope — evaluative dignity finding

pairs.left: A carousel auto-advances past 5 seconds with no pause control
pairs.right: Inside WCAG conformance scope (2.2.2)

pairs.left: A task requires 14 taps when 6 would achieve the same outcome
pairs.right: Outside formal conformance scope — evaluative energy-cost finding

hints: Ask whether a specific, numbered WCAG success criterion actually addresses the mechanism in each finding.
Missing labels and auto-advancing motion both map directly onto named, testable criteria; physical kiosk placement and interaction counts don't.
explanation: A missing programmatic label and an uncontrollable auto-advancing carousel both map directly onto specific, testable WCAG success criteria (4.1.2 and 2.2.2 respectively). A kiosk's physical placement and an interaction count are both real, checkable findings this track has built the skills to write — but neither maps onto a numbered conformance criterion, which is exactly why they're reported as evaluative findings, honestly labelled as such, rather than either dropped or forced under a citation that doesn't actually fit.

prompt: Put these steps in order for evaluating whether a requested piece of sensitive information is justified.

items: State the specific purpose the field is meant to serve
Ask whether the immediate task the user is completing right now actually requires it, not just whether it could be useful eventually
If a purpose is genuine, check whether a narrower version (a threshold, a yes/no) could serve it as well as the exact value
Check who actually receives or can see the answer, and whether that's scoped to who needs it

hints: Start with what the field claims to be for, before checking whether that claim survives scrutiny.
Routing is the final check — it only matters once you've already established the field is genuinely needed in some form.
explanation: Stating the purpose first is what makes the rest checkable — a field with no purpose at all fails immediately, as the lesson's photo-upload example showed. Testing against the immediate task filters out 'might be useful someday' framing. Checking for a narrower equivalent (threshold versus exact value) catches over-collection even where a real purpose exists. And checking routing last makes sense structurally — routing only matters once a field has already survived the necessity tests, since a field that shouldn't exist at all doesn't need its routing evaluated.

prompt: A software subscription's cancellation flow is a single screen with one retention offer and a plainly-labelled 'Cancel now' button — but the retention offer's discount amount is deliberately left blank until the user hovers over it for two full seconds, described internally as 'building anticipation.' Evaluate whether this is a dark pattern, and if so, name the closest fit among the patterns covered in this module (or state that it's a different, unnamed pattern).
hints: This doesn't cleanly match confirmshaming (no loaded language) or roach motel (exit isn't actually harder than entry) — consider whether it's still worth flagging as its own thing.
Think about whose interest the deliberate delay serves, and whether the delay itself achieves anything for the user.
explanation: A strong answer: *This doesn't cleanly match confirmshaming (no loaded language on any option) or roach motel (the actual cancel action is a single, plainly labelled button, not a multi-screen exit). It's still worth flagging as a distinct, deliberate friction pattern — an artificial delay serving no functional purpose for the user, added specifically to manufacture engagement with a retention offer the user may not even want to see, on a screen whose actual task (cancelling) doesn't require it at all.* Whether or not it maps to a single named pattern from this lesson, the underlying test still applies: does this delay serve the user's actual task, or does it exist purely to serve the business's retention interest at the cost of the user's time and attention — and the honest answer here is the second, which is enough to justify naming it as a finding even without a perfect label from the two patterns this lesson covered by name.
